x: ← Project Scroll About About Project Scroll Project Scroll is independent historical research: an online treasure hunt anyone can play, a research desk anyone can hire, and a studio for digital imaging, design, photography, 3D LiDAR, animation and video. All of it runs on one rule. Every clue is true, and every answer is in the record. Who we are Project Scroll is run by an independent researcher and author who writes narrative nonfiction about the history of the Great Lakes country, and who trained in visual communications. The research behind that writing is the same research we offer you: old certificates, deeds, surveys, county histories and newspapers, read line by line and compared until they agree, or until we can say exactly why they don’t. What we offer Professional research. Lost ancestors, family histories and registers, family legends tested against the record, forgotten places, maps and land surveys, heirlooms, lodges and old societies, historical research for authors, films and local groups, and a second pair of eyes on anything you mean to publish. Research services . Imaging, design and video. Digital imaging of photographs, documents, maps and heirlooms; imaging analysis of faded ink, damaged pages and the details in old photographs; image creation and restoration; graphic design for family books, charts, covers and keepsakes; photography; and video production, from family-history films to recorded interviews. 3D and living documents. Landscapes modeled in three dimensions from public LiDAR elevation surveys, 3D animations and fly-throughs, every reconstruction labeled as one, and living documents: research papers, timelines and family records that keep growing as new evidence turns up, with every change dated. The studio . Every commission starts with an honest first read: what can be done, and what it will take, before you commit to anything. What we believe The record decides. Not the family tree online, not the story everybody tells, not what we hoped to find. Every statement is marked. You can always see whether a fact comes from a document, a book, a family story or our own reading. How we mark the evidence . Gaps are shown, not filled. An honest “not yet known” is worth more than a confident guess. Corrections are welcome. If you know better, tell us. The record is bigger than any one of us. Places and people are respected. The hunt never asks anyone to dig, to disturb a grave or a mound, or to go looking for anyone’s home. When we get something wrong We will. When a reader or a new document shows that a page of this site is mistaken, we change the page, date the change on it, and say what was wrong, rather than quietly replacing the words. A case that was called solved on a bad reading is reopened and says so. If you have found an error, write to research@projectscroll.com or tell us on Facebook; corrections are credited to the person who sent them, by name or not, as they prefer. The record behind this site The dates on the scroll, the person of the month and the then-and-now maps are built from the same sources the hunt asks you to open: Rogers (1875), Mathews (1882), Glover (1906), the 1860 wall map at the Library of Congress, and Michigan death certificates at the Archives of Michigan. Where a page of this site makes a claim, the source is on the page or one click away. If it is not, that is a correction we owe. Where it started Project Scroll began in Cassopolis, Michigan , with a few questions the county history couldn’t answer. It doesn’t stop there. The hunt and the desk now take on questions from anywhere the records reach. ← Project Scroll For every reader Accessibility The hunt is open to anyone, anywhere, and that includes anyone who reads with a keyboard, a screen reader, a magnifier, captions or a steady page. We aim to meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 at level AA, and we test every change against them. What is built in Keyboard. Every link, button, filter, map control and dialog works from the keyboard. A “Skip to the content” link is the first thing on every page. Press / or Ctrl K to search. Screen readers. Pages use real headings, landmarks and labels. Pictures carry text descriptions; decorative ornaments are hidden from screen readers. Motion. If your device asks for reduced motion, the gold leaf, glints, rolling place names and drawn trails hold still. The Pause all motion switch at the foot of every page does the same on any device, and remembers your choice. Light and dark. The site follows your device, and the moon button switches by hand. Text and controls are checked for contrast in both. Listening. The Listen buttons read a section aloud with your device’s own voice. Text size. Zoom to 200% or more and the page reflows to one column without sideways scrolling. Print. Every page prints cleanly, without the animations and controls. What is harder, and how we help The deep-zoom maps in the map room are pictures served by the Library of Congress. Their town names and directories are given in text beside them, and we will read any part of a map for you on request. Old handwriting and print. Certificates and book pages are shown as pictures. Where a page is the subject of a case, its key lines are transcribed in the text; ask, and we will transcribe any page you need. Facebook. Clues are posted on Facebook, whose accessibility is Meta’s. Every case also has its own page here. Tell us If anything on Project Scroll is hard to use, write to research@projectscroll.com with the page and what happened. We answer, and we fix what we can. ← Project Scroll This day in the valley The valley’s almanac 95 days the county histories remember to the date: a first train, a first newspaper, a fire, a charter, a church dedicated. Every one carries the book and page it comes from, so you can open the record and read it yourself. Jan · Feb · Mar · Apr · May · Jun · Jul · Aug · Sep · Oct · Nov · Dec January 1 January, 1835 Mishawaka. Voters at St. Joseph Iron Works (later Mishawaka) elected village trustees, the first village organization in St. Joseph County. History of St. Joseph County, Indiana (Chapman, 1880), p. 790 2 January, 1864 Dowagiac. A great fire destroyed more than half of Dowagiac's business district. Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), p. 197 4 January, 1869 Niles. The new iron bridge over the St. Joseph River at Niles was completed and accepted by the city's Board of Aldermen. History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties, Michigan (D. W. Ensign, 1880), p. 160 7 January, 1866 Dowagiac. A fire that began in the Stebbins store swept along Dowagiac's Commercial and Front streets. Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), p. 198 8 January, 1900 Cassopolis. The building committee reported that Cass County's new courthouse at Cassopolis was substantially finished. Glover, A Twentieth Century History of Cass County, Michigan (1906), p. 211 13 January, 1850 Niles. The Presbyterian congregation at Niles dedicated its new church, built in 1849. History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties, Michigan (D. W. Ensign, 1880), p. 163 16 January, 1871 Cassopolis. Regular passenger trains began running on the new Air Line railroad through Cassopolis. Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), p. 80 28 January, 1837 Goshen. The first number of the Goshen Express was issued. History of Elkhart County, Indiana (Chapman, 1881), p. 605 30 January, 1896 Dowagiac. The Tourists' Club of Dowagiac was organized. Glover, A Twentieth Century History of Cass County, Michigan (1906), p. 341 February 2 February, 1836 Edwardsburg. Citizens met at Edwardsburg about a canal from Constantine to Niles; most of those present favored a railroad. Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), p. 79 2 February, 1870 St. Joseph. The railroad from St. Joseph to New Buffalo opened for traffic, and St. Joseph held a grand celebration. History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties, Michigan (D. W. Ensign, 1880), p. 55 3 February, 1858 Dowagiac. The Board of Supervisors incorporated Dowagiac as a village. (Glover 1906, p. 156, gives February 1, 1858.) Rogers, History of Cass County (1875), p. 268 6 February, 1836 Niles. Citizens met to ask for a charter for a 'Bank of Niles'. History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties, Michigan (D. W. Ensign, 1880), p. 169 9 February, 1871 Cassopolis. Rails of the Peninsular railway line reached Cassopolis. Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), p. 80 11 February, 1871 Cassopolis. The Cassopolis library and reading-room society was incorporated under state law. Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), p. 173 12 February, 1835 Niles. The legislative act incorporating the village of Niles was approved. History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties, Michigan (D. W. Ensign, 1880), p. 161 12 February, 1859 Niles. Niles received its city charter. History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties, Michigan (D. W. Ensign, 1880), p. 161 14 February, 1863 St. Joseph. The first number of the St. Joseph Pioneer newspaper was issued. History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties, Michigan (D. W. Ensign, 1880), p. 139 16 February, 1848 Dowagiac. The plat of the new village of Dowagiac was recorded at the Register's office in Cassopolis. Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), p. 182 21 February, 1838 Niles. The Niles Intelligencer began publication after the Niles Gazette collapsed. History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties, Michigan (D. W. Ensign, 1880), p. 137 24 February, 1846 Bristol. A fire at Bristol burned G. G. Lansing's store and other propert

← Project Scroll Your field book Your tin badges In the winter of 1846–47, two hundred badges of the “Ancient and Honorable Order” were worn at a ball in Cassopolis. Not one is known to survive. Here you can earn your own: twenty-three of them: twenty for the things you do as you explore the site, two for keeping the hunt going, and one for cracking a case, with five ranks on the way from Candidate to Keeper of the Hall. Say the word Somewhere on every page of this site, a line is written in code. Turn it with the cipher wheel in the hunter’s toolkit , and it will tell you what to do. The word The second line You broke the first. Here is a harder one, and the cipher wheel alone will not open it. Look at the wheel’s other setting. GSV HVXLMW DLIW RH XSZIGVI. ML DSVVO DROO GFIM RG. SLOW RG GL Z NRIILI. The second word Carry your ledger Your badges, followed cases and notebook live only in this browser. To carry them to another device, take your ledger with you: a small file, made here, that Project Scroll on another device can read back. Nothing is sent to us. Bring a ledger back Your charter Every badge earned. You may print your charter: type your name as you want it written, then print. Your name Your charter is made on this device. Nothing is sent anywhere. Project Scroll Charter of the Hall Know all by these presents that having read the walls, followed the record, broken both ciphers and earned every one of the tin badges, is hereby received as Keeper of the Hall with all the honor and none of the dignity that any such title has ever carried. Every clue is true. Every answer is in the record. Your badges are kept only in this browser, on this device. Nobody else can see them, and we never receive them. ← Project Scroll Cass County, Michigan Cassopolis, Michigan: its history, in the record Cassopolis is the county seat of Cass County, Michigan, platted in 1831 and named for Lewis Cass, then governor of Michigan Territory. This page gathers what Project Scroll has opened so far on the village and its county: the maps, the county histories, the certificates and the newspapers, with a link to each record where it is held. The village at a glance Founded: platted 1831; chosen as county seat the same year, a compromise between rival settlements. Named for: Lewis Cass (1782–1866), governor of Michigan Territory 1813–31, later Secretary of War and of State. First published histories: Howard S. Rogers, History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 (Cassopolis, 1875); Alfred Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (Chicago, 1882); L. H. Glover, A Twentieth Century History of Cass County (Chicago, 1906). On the map: the 1860 Geil & Harley wall map of Cass County, held by the Library of Congress, carries a plan of the village with lot numbers and owners; you can lay it over today’s streets , and the county’s township sheets of about 1928 are in the map room . Vital records: Michigan death certificates from 1897 are free to read at the Archives of Michigan; here is how to read one . Who kept the village in 1860: two hotels, three merchants and three physicians, engraved beside the Cassopolis plan on the county wall map. Geil, Harley & Siverd, 1860 · Library of Congress What the hunt has found in Cassopolis The hunt began here, with a joke secret society of 1846 whose story is told in Rogers and Mathews, a village hotel that was hauled across town and turned into a mill, and a doctor who kept a bone. Each is an open case on the case board ; the first two are listed here, and each has its sources free online. Who told Shepard the story of the 1846 lodge? Where did the Union Hotel go when it became a mill? Document of the month: one page of Rogers, 1875, read slowly A field note: one letter, two certificates Next door, 1860 and 1928 Penn Township is the ground just east of the village, with Diamond Lake in its south-west corner and Vandalia on the railroad. Here it is twice: as the 1860 wall map engraved it, and as a plat book drew it about 1928. The square mile sections are the same, so the two line up. Slide across and watch sixty-eight years of owners change hands. 1860 c. 1928 Penn Township, 1860 and about 1928. Geil, Harley & Siverd, 1860, Library of Congress · plat book, about 1928, Cass County MIGenWeb A challenge Find the families who stayed Ten surnames are written on this township in both years: on a farm in 1860, and still on the land about 1928. Find them. Slide the map, read the names, and type each one you find. A surname on both maps The hotel corner, thirty years on In 1860 the engraver wrote one word on the block by the court house: HOTEL. Twenty-four years later the Sanborn Map Company drew the same corner building by building, for the insurers. The court house and post office face Broadway, the county jail and the sheriff’s house stand behind them, and across the street stands a hotel under a name the 1860 directory never lists. Is it on the ground where the 1860 hotel stood? Lay the two maps side by side and decide for yourself. Broadway and State, November 1884: the court house and post office, the jail, the county offices and the Exchange House. Pink is brick, yellow is wood. Open the whole sheet , or step through the 1892, 1899 and 1909 editions in the map room. ← Project Scroll For teachers Project Scroll for classrooms New: the teachers’ pack. A one-day field trip to Cassopolis (the Broadway walk, the Local History Branch and the photo spots), with two printable worksheets: rephotographing an old postcard, and reading an old record. Download the teachers’ pack (PDF) Four ready lessons in local history and map reading, built on the real maps, directories and county histories of the St. Joseph River Valley. Free, nothing to sign up for, and nothing collected from students. Print this page and go. Then and now Grades 3 and up · 40 minutes · Map reading, change over time You need: Seven towns, then and now and a screen or printed copies. Choose a town near your school. Open its page and fade slowly from the old plan to today. List three things that are still there (a street, a square, a river crossing) and three that are gone. Find the street that changed its name, using the challenge on the page. Talk about it: why might a town rename a street? Who decides? Going further: Walk the street, if you can, with the “Where am I?” button on a phone, and photograph what stands there now. Who was in town Grades 4 to 8 · 45 minutes · Primary sources as data, graphs You need: Who was in town and a screen or printed copies. Pick one town’s 1860 or 1861 business directory. Sort the entries into trades: law, medicine, food, building, transport, making things. Make a bar graph of the trades. Which town had the most lawyers? The most shoemakers? Ask: who is missing from a directory that people paid to be listed in? (Most farmers, labourers, women and children.) Going further: Compare two towns, or a directory of today, and write what changed. This day in the valley Grades 6 to 12 · 45 minutes · Primary and secondary sources, citation You need: The valley’s almanac and a screen or printed copies. Find the almanac entry nearest to today’s date, or a student’s birthday. Open the county history page it cites. Read the whole paragraph around the date. Decide: was the writer there? How many years after the event did they write? Who told them? Write a one-sentence citation for the source, with book, year and page. Going further: Look for the same event in a newspaper of the time and compare the two accounts. Weighing the evidence Grades 6 to 12 · 50 minutes · Evaluating sources, reasoning from evidence You need: Reading gravestones and the death certificate guide and a screen or printed copies. Read the guide together. List who made a gravestone, a death certificate and a county history, and when. Give pairs a disagreement: an age on a stone and an age on a certificate that differ by a year. Each pair decides which to trust and writes why, using the guide’s questions. Share: what extra record would settle it? Going further: Play one of the open cases on the case board as a class, and post the class’s answer. Notes for teachers Every source is public domain and credited where it is held. Students can open the original every time. The junior hunt , seven questions answered from the maps and directories, makes a good warm-up: Junior surveyors . Nothing to dig, nowhere to trespass. Every answer is in a book, a map or a record. Please teach the same rule on any field trip. Ideas, corrections, or a class that solved a case? Write to research@projectscroll.com . ← Project Scroll Document of the month · October 2026 One page of Rogers, 1875 Every month we put one real page on the table and read it slowly. This month: page 253 of Howard S. Rogers’s History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 , the first time the joke lodge of 1846 was ever printed, with the man who told it to Rogers only a footnote away. Rogers, 1875, p. 253. The boxed paragraphs are the lodge story. Tap or click the page to see it full size. What it is Rogers was Cass County’s first historian. His book came out in 1875, fifty years after the county’s first land entries, while people who had seen 1846 were still alive to be asked. That is the book’s value and its danger at once: it is close to the events, and it is made of what people remembered. How to read it Read past the quotation. Rogers quotes a long passage and then adds a few words of his own. The words after the closing quotation mark are where a careful reader slows down. Watch the punctuation. On the next page a single question mark sits inside a parenthesis. A question mark in a county history is a historian telling you, as plainly as he dared, that he is not sure. Find the teller. The passage is a quotation, and Rogers was not there in 1846. Seven years later Alfred Mathews reprinted the passage and put the teller’s name in a footnote: James M. Shepard, who was three years old in 1846. Who told him? Count what can be counted. Two hundred badges, one ball, one winter. Each number is a thing that might have left a record somewhere else: a newspaper, a bill, a diary, a badge in a drawer. Read it yourself The whole book is free online in the University of Michigan’s county-histories collection: Rogers, History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 . Go to pages 253–254. Then compare Mathews, 1882 , page 174, where the same story is printed again, and notice what is missing. This page is the opening clue of Case 1 . If you read it closely enough, you may not need the rest. Next month This is the first document of the month. The next is chosen on the first of November. ← The places Cass County, Michigan Dowagiac, Michigan: its history, in the record Dowagiac grew where the Michigan Central Railroad crossed Dowagiac Creek in 1848, and was incorporated as a village in 1863 and a city in 1877. Its name is Potawatomi, from a word usually read as “fishing water.” It became the county’s manufacturing town: the Round Oak Stove works, founded by P. D. Beckwith in 1871, and the grain drills of the Dowagiac Manufacturing Company. The town at a glance Founded: settled at the railroad crossing, 1848; village 1863; city 1877. Name: Potawatomi, for the creek; several spellings in the early record. In the county histories: Rogers (1875), Mathews (1882) and Glover (1906) each give the village its own chapter, with the first merchants, mills and churches named. On the map: the 1860 wall map carries a plan of Dowagiac with its lots; lay it over today’s streets . Industry: Round Oak stoves from 1871; at its height in the 1910s the works employed about 1,200 of the town’s 5,000 people. On old postcards Beckwith Building, Dowagiac, Mich · 1912, C. R. Childs Tinder Collection, Clements Library, University of Michigan · source M.C. R.R. Station, Dowagiac, Mich · 1910, Will P. Canaan Co. Tinder Collection, Clements Library, University of Michigan · source M. C. Railway and Drill Works, Dowagiac, Mich · 1912 Tinder Collection, Clements Library, University of Michigan · source Our New Fire Truck, Homecoming Aug. 1912, Dowagiac, Mich · 1912 Tinder Collection, Clements Library, University of Michigan · source From public-domain postcards and photographs, each linked to the library that holds it. See them all . Where to look Dowagiac’s records are thick: a weekly press from the 1860s and a daily later, the Round Oak company papers, and city directories from the 1890s that list the heads of every household. The desk reads them for Cass County families as a matter of course. The records page links each source where it is held, and the glossary explains the words the old records use. ← Research services Research services Family histories, built to be checked Most family trees are copied from other family trees. Ours are built from the records themselves: every name, date and place marked with where it came from, every gap shown honestly, and every family story kept exactly as it was told, beside the evidence that tests it. What we make Looking down A family register Every descendant of one couple, generation by generation, each person given a number, so that a reader can follow any branch from the first settlers to the present day. The form genealogists have trusted for 150 years. Looking back An ancestral monograph Your ancestors, back as far as the records honestly go, on a single chart. Where a line stops, it says whose parents are wanting, so you can see at a glance what is known, what is not, and where to look next. The whole story A family history Every line written up as a story, with the evidence beneath it: maps, records, a list of every source, an index of names and places, and the open questions set out for the next person to take up. A specimen monograph Here is how an ancestral monograph works, using an invented family. Tap anyone to see what we know about them, and how we know it. Specimen. The names are invented; the method is real. Tap a name in the chart. “Clara ?” A question mark means the marriage is recorded but her own surname is not. Women are usually recorded under their husbands’ names, which is not the same as being born with them. “Wanting” An empty box beside a known person is a real gap: someone we could find tomorrow. The boxes beyond the edge of the chart, behind Clara’s missing parents, are not gaps at all. There is nothing to look for there until her parents are found. The warning sign. When two records cannot both be true, the chart flags the joint and leaves it in. Never solve a problem by deleting the evidence. How a register reads 1. AUGUST¹ BRANDT was born about 1862 Inference and died in 1931 Document . He married WILHELMINA KRAUSE , born in 1866 Document . Children of August and Wilhelmina: + 2 i. OTTO² , born 1890; married CLARA ? ii. Emma, born 1893; died 1894, aged one. The small raised number is the generation. The plus sign means Otto’s own family is carried forward under his number, 2, so a reader can follow his line on down without losing the thread. (The same invented family as the chart above.) Lessons from our own desk Every one learned the hard way, on a family history built at this desk. A woman dies under her married name. For years a death certificate went unfound because everyone searched for her under her maiden name. It was filed under her husband’s. Search the unusual name. A rare surname finds the family and almost nobody else. A common one needs a place and a date beside it, or it finds thousands. A strong lead in the right county is still not a parent. A well-documented man of the right name, in the right place, at the right time, turned out to be no relation at all. The answer was in a different family. An abstract is not a record. A published summary of a colonial will gave two witnesses’ names and a probate date. The court’s own record disagreed on both. “About” must stay “about.” A birth year worked out from an age at death was printed beside real dates, and soon looked like one. Estimates are marked as estimates, always. The best finds are in free books nobody opened. Lines written off as dead ends turned out to be answered in county histories and family genealogies that had been free online for years. Dead ends don’t get searched. Starting your family’s history Tell us who. One couple to work down from, or one person to work back from. Names, places, rough dates. Send what the family has. Bible pages, letters, photographs, obituaries, old trees. We read every one, and we keep every family story exactly as it was told. Agree on the shape. A register, a monograph, a full history, or a single line to begin with. We build it from the records. Ce

← Project Scroll From the desk The glossary The words old records use, and the words we use about them, in plain English. Learn a handful, and an old deed or gravestone starts to talk. Find a word Abstract A summary of a document, such as a deed or will, giving its main points. Useful for finding the original, but not the record itself: abstracts drop words and sometimes get names and dates wrong. Administrator The person a court appoints to settle the estate of someone who died without a will. Compare executor. Ahnentafel German for “ancestor table.” A numbering system for a pedigree: the subject is 1, a person’s father is double their number and their mother double plus one. So 2 is the father, 3 the mother, 4 the father’s father. Census A count of the population. The United States has taken one every ten years since 1790; from 1850 it names every free person in the household (enslaved people were counted on separate schedules, usually without names, until 1870). Most of the 1890 census was destroyed after a fire in 1921. Each census is opened to the public 72 years after it was taken. Consort A husband or wife. Often seen on old gravestones: “Mary, consort of John Smith.” County history The big county histories printed from the 1870s to the 1910s. Many biographies in them were paid for by the people they describe, so they tend to be reliable on what the family knew well, and generous on everything else; dates and places still need a document. Deed The written record of land changing hands, copied into the county’s deed books. Deeds often name wives, heirs and neighbors, and sometimes say where a seller had moved to. Ditto (do.) “The same as above.” Census takers and clerks used it, or a pair of marks, for repeated surnames, birthplaces and occupations. Double dating Dates such as “10 February 1731/2.” Before 1752, England and its colonies began the new year on 25 March, so January to March dates were often written with both years. Et ux. Latin, “and wife,” in deeds and court records: “John Smith et ux.” means John and his wife. Executor The person named in a will to carry it out. Compare administrator. Field notes A surveyor’s notebook from the original land survey, recording every line walked: the trees, streams, soil and sometimes the people met along the way. General Land Office The federal office that surveyed and sold public land, from 1812 until it became part of the Bureau of Land Management in 1946. Its plats, field notes and patents are free online. Informant The person who answered the questions on a certificate. On a death certificate the dead person was never the informant, so everything on it is someone else’s memory. Instant and ultimo Old newspaper shorthand: “the 4th inst.” means the 4th of this month; “the 20th ult.” the 20th of last month. Intestate Having died without a will. The court then appoints an administrator and divides the estate by law. Land patent The first transfer of a piece of land from the government to a private owner. Local legend The famous ancestor, the buried treasure, the river under the ground. Some are true. The desk reads each one against the record and says which. Long s (ſ) An s that looks like an f without the full crossbar, used at the start or in the middle of a word until about 1800. “Congreſs” is Congress. Lore What a place says about itself: the stories passed around a lake, a township or a lodge, told without a page to point to. Lore is where a hunt often starts; the record is where it ends. Maiden name A woman’s surname before marriage. Most records name married women only by their husbands’ surnames, which is why a woman’s own family is the commonest gap in any tree. mtDNA and Y-DNA Two DNA tests that follow one line each: mitochondrial DNA passes from mother to child down the all-female line; Y-DNA passes from father to son down the all-male line. Naturalization The process of becoming a citizen. Older files often have two parts: a declaration of intention (“first paper

t: How do I read a Michigan death certificate?
x: ← Project Scroll A guide from the desk How do I read a Michigan death certificate? A death certificate is two records in one. The doctor wrote down the death, at the time. Someone else, the informant, answered questions about a whole life, on the hardest day. Tap any numbered box to see who filled it in, and how far to trust it. Box 11 Informant Filled in by: How far to trust it: Every box, in order The rule of thumb The top half (boxes 3 to 10) is memory : what the informant believed about a life. The bottom half (boxes 12 to 16) is the event : written by people who were there that week. When either half disagrees with another record, trust the bottom half first, and weigh the top half by who the informant was. Remember: the dead person was never the informant. Everything in the top half is someone else’s memory, given on the hardest day, so find the informant’s name on the certificate and ask how well they knew the life they were describing. Michigan’s certificates from 1897 to 1952 are free to view at the Archives of Michigan . Elsewhere, try FamilySearch or your state archives. t: How do I read an old gravestone?
x: ← The hunter’s toolkit A guide from the desk Reading old gravestones A gravestone is a record, cut in stone by a family that wanted to be remembered. It is also often wrong: carved years after the death, from memory, by a stonecutter paid by the letter. Here is how to read one, and how far to trust it. What the stone is telling you willow · urn Willow and urn A weeping willow over an urn: mourning, carved most often from about the 1790s to the 1850s. A rough date for a stone whose numbers have worn away. lamb A lamb Usually a child’s grave. Lambs on small stones are among the commonest carvings of the 1800s. a hand A hand pointing up Hope of heaven. A hand reaching down from a cloud is God calling the soul home; it does not mean a sudden death, though it is often read that way. two hands Clasped hands A farewell, or a marriage. Look at the cuffs: a man’s and a woman’s sleeve mean husband and wife. FLT Three linked rings The Odd Fellows, a fraternal order: Friendship, Love and Truth. A lead to a lodge’s records and its burial benefit. square · compass Square and compass The Freemasons. Like the rings, it points to a lodge that may have kept minutes and paid for the funeral. G.A.R. A bronze star or flag holder The Grand Army of the Republic, the society of Union veterans of the Civil War. The man was a soldier; look for his regiment. a shield A marble stone with a sunk shield A government headstone for a Union soldier, with his company and regiment cut in the shield: the key to his service record and pension file. ætat · æ In the 74th year of his age “Ætat.” or “æ.” means aged. “In the 74th year of his age” means he was 73: the 74th year began on his 73rd birthday. 23y 4m 12d Ages to the day Age in years, months and days. Count back from the date of death to the birth date with the age calculator . consort · relict Wife or widow “Consort of” means his wife, who died while he lived. “Relict of” means his widow, who outlived him. marble · granite What it is made of Marble, white or grey, was usual from about the 1830s to 1900 and dissolves slowly in the rain, so its letters soften. Granite took over from the late 1800s. A hollow, blue-grey stone with crisp letters is “white bronze”, cast zinc, sold from the 1870s to about 1914. How far to trust a stone When was it carved? Many stones were put up years after the burial, and a family stone listing several people was often cut all at once, long after the first death. The dates on it are memories. Who paid for it? The family, so the stone says what the family believed: the age they remembered, the spelling they used. Check it against a record made at the time: a death certificate, a church burial register, a newspaper notice, the cemetery’s own book. Where they disagree, the record made at the time usually wins. See how to read a death certificate . A missing stone is not a missing grave. Wooden markers rotted, stones broke and were cleared away, and many people never had a stone at all. Reading a worn stone, without harming it Use raking light. Hold a mirror or a torch low and to one side so the light skims across the face; the letters appear in shadow. Try different times of day. Photograph it straight on and at an angle, with the light coming from several sides. Never use shaving cream, flour, chalk, bleach, wire brushes or household cleaners. They stay in the stone and eat it. Do not make rubbings of soft, flaking or leaning stones; on a sound stone, ask the cemetery first. Leave it as you found it. Do not lean on stones, prop them up or move pieces. Report damage to the cemetery’s keeper. Be a good visitor Keep to the paths and the cemetery’s hours, and ask permission before entering a private family plot. Never dig, probe or disturb the ground, and never take anything away. It is wrong, and in Michigan and Indiana, as elsewhere, it can be a crime. No case on Project Scroll ever needs it. Remember the families. The people buried here have descendants nearby. t: How do I read old handwriting in records?
x: ← The hunter’s toolkit A guide from the desk How do I read old handwriting in records? The writing in old records is not hard once you know ten tricks the clerks used. Here they are, with a short quiz at the end. The clerks’ tricks ſ The long s Looks like an f without the full crossbar. Used at the start or middle of a word until about 1800: “Congreſs”, “ſon”, “Miſsiſsippi”. Read it as an ordinary s. ye “Ye” means “the” The y stands for an old letter, thorn (þ), pronounced “th”. “Ye olde inn” was always read “the old inn”. Likewise “yt” = that, “ym” = them. Wm · Jno · Chas Shortened first names Clerks raised the last letters: Wm = William, Jno = John (not Jonathan), Chas = Charles, Thos = Thomas, Jas = James, Geo = George, Saml = Samuel, Benj = Benjamin. inst. · ult. · prox. Which month? “The 4th inst.” = the 4th of this month. “The 20th ult.” = the 20th of last month. “The 2nd prox.” = the 2nd of next month. Check the date of the letter or newspaper to know which month. do. Ditto “do.” under an entry means “the same as above.” Census takers and clerks used it for repeated surnames, birthplaces and occupations. &c. Et cetera The ampersand plus c: “and so on”. Often written as a looped sign that can look like a letter. 1745/6 Double dates Before 1752 in England and its colonies, the new year began on 25 March. A date between January and March is often written with both years. Use the later one for today’s calendar. relict · consort On gravestones “Relict of John Smith” = his widow (she outlived him). “Consort of” = his wife, who died while he was living. dec’d · Esq. In deeds and wills dec’d = deceased. Esq. = Esquire, a courtesy for a lawyer or a man of standing, not a title of nobility. 71y 4m 12d Ages to the day Age at death in years, months and days. Count back from the date of death with the age calculator . Test yourself Six questions. A letter dated 10 June says “your note of the 28th ult.” When was the note written? “ult.” means last month: 28 May. In a 1790 newspaper you read “Congreſs”. What does it say? That f-like letter is the long s. A census line reads “Jno Smith” and below it “do. do.” What is the second person’s name? Jno is John, and do. repeats the line above. A gravestone reads “Mary, relict of Amos Hale.” What does it tell you? A relict outlived her husband. A baptism is dated “12 February 1734/5”. Which year is it on today’s calendar? Use the later year for January to March dates before 1752. “Ye Olde Tavern” was read aloud as… The y stands for the old letter thorn, “th”. Part IV Bring us your mystery Some questions have waited a hundred years for someone to look properly. If the answer was ever written down, we will look for it, and tell you honestly what we find. When what you have is a faded photograph, a fragile page or a story worth showing, the studio can image, restore, design, model or film it. Cases from our desk A pioneer whose death certificate and his son’s can’t agree on his middle initial. A lake the 1882 county history said was fed by a river running underground from Lake Superior. A small-town doctor’s 1849 trek to the California gold fields, and a typescript of it listed in a museum’s collection, still waiting to be read for the hunt. Two certificates Michigan death certificates, 1912 and 1935, Archives of Michigan. The father’s own certificate gives no middle initial; his son’s, filled in twenty-three years later, gives him one. Part V Five promises Five promises we keep on every case and commission, whether it takes an afternoon or a season. Every claim comes with its source. You’ll know exactly where each fact came from, so you can check it yourself. Disagreements are clues, not failures. When two records argue, we show you both and explain why. Open questions stay open. If something might be true but can’t be proven yet, we say so, and we keep looking instead of throwing it away. No guarantees, just the record. Some questions have answers on paper and some don’t. We’ll tell you up front which kind yours looks like. We research the past. No locating living people, no legal or title opinions, no appraisals. No digging, no trespassing, and care with every family’s story. State of Michigan, record of deaths, Allegan County. We read the page itself, not someone’s summary of it. What you get A written report in plain English: what we found, where we found it, what is still open, and where to look next. Where the old books and maps are free online, we include the links so you can turn the pages yourself. For studio work, you get the finished images, design files or film, and your originals back as you sent them. See a sample report .

Part VI How we mark the evidence Not every source is worth the same. A death certificate filed the week a man died is not a story his grandson told sixty years later, and neither of them is our own opinion. So in every research report, every statement carries one of nine marks, strongest first. You can see at a glance what the record says, and what we are arguing from it. Strongest Weakest What the record says What we argue from it What the record says Document Made at the time, by someone whose job was to write it down: a death certificate, a deed, a census page, a survey, a map. Example: a 1912 Michigan death certificate. Period print Printed at or near the time: a newspaper notice, an obituary, a book of the day. Example: a doctor’s obituary printed the year he died. County history The big county histories of the 1870s to the 1910s. Rich and indispensable, but often written decades later from what families remembered, and rarely checked. Example: the 1882 History of Cass County. Compiled A later hand gathering earlier records: an index, a bibliography, a transcription, a modern summary. Good for finding things; we go back to the original whenever it survives. Example: a trail-diary bibliography that lists an unpublished typescript. Tradition What a family or a community says, passed down by word of mouth. Worth recording exactly as told, and worth testing. Example: “Grandpa always said he came over on the last boat before the war.” Field What we saw or measured ourselves, at first hand, dated, from public ground or with permission. Example: a dated photograph of a marker on a public roadside. What we argue from it Inference A step that follows directly from the records. Example: one certificate was filed a month after he died, the other twenty-three years later, so the first informant was closer to the event. Reading Our interpretation of what the records point to. Always labeled, always open to correction. Example: “In 1935, someone gave the father his son’s initial.” Hypothesis An idea worth testing that the records don’t yet support. We say what would prove or disprove it. Example: he never used a middle initial at all; his obituary and gravestone would tell. Marks, strongest first: Document Period print County history Compiled Tradition Field (seen at first hand) Inference Reading Hypothesis — the last three marks are our own argument, offered for correction How it looks in a report A pioneer died in Michigan in 1912. His death certificate gives no middle initial Document . A county history adds “Senior” to his name County history . His son’s death certificate, filled in twenty-three years later, gives the father a middle initial: the son’s own Document . The first informant was closer to the event Inference . Father and son shared a name, and in 1935 someone gave the father the son’s initial too Reading . Or he never used a middle initial at all, which his obituary would show Hypothesis . Tap a mark to see what it means. From our case “ One Letter, Two Certificates .” Every report you receive from us is marked the same way. Weigh the evidence Add records to each side and watch the scale. Records are weighed, not counted: one good document can outweigh a pile of family stories. Side A Side B The scale is level. Add a record to either side. The weights are a rule of thumb, not a formula: a late or careless document can still be wrong, and a detailed tradition can still be right. Try marking these yourself Teachers and group leaders are welcome to use this exercise and the hunter’s worksheet in class. Tell us how it went. Pick the mark you would give each one. A notice in the local paper, the week after he died. Period print. It was printed at the time, but by a newspaper, not by an office whose job was to record the death. “Great-aunt Ruth always said the family came from Ohio.” Tradition. Write it down exactly as she said it, then go and test it. A website listing every burial in a cemetery, typed up by volunteers. Comp

Part VII From the field notes Lesson No. 1 from the desk: two old records, two different stories. Here is what to do. Ask who gave the information, and when. Closer to the event usually weighs more, but not always. Keep looking. A third, independent record can tip the balance, but records are weighed, not counted. Write down both versions and where each came from. Never quietly “fix” one. Call it settled only when the evidence settles it. Until then, it’s an open question. From “One Letter, Two Certificates.” Read the whole case · All field notes Person of the month · October James M. Shepard, the dentist who wrote it down He was three years old in 1846, when the joke lodge was founded. He came to Cassopolis in 1868 and worked there as a dentist. In September 1870 the village’s reading room was organized in his dental office, and a year later he was one of the incorporators of its library association. When Howard Rogers wrote the county’s first history in 1875, it was Shepard who wrote down the story of the lodge: the halters, the blindfolds, the ball and the two hundred badges. Seven years later, Alfred Mathews reprinted it and named him in a footnote. On the record: in the same winter of 1846–47 that the joke lodge held its ball, the Odd Fellows’ Cass County Lodge No. 21 received its dispensation; Rogers called it “the first legitimate secret society.” The open question. He was three in 1846. Who told him? Sources: Howard S. Rogers, History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 (1875), pp. 253–254 and 258; A. Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), p. 174. Part VIII Questions people ask Search the questions No question matches that yet. Email us or ask on Facebook . Does the hunt cost anything? No. The hunt is free to follow and free to play. All you need is curiosity and, now and then, a library card. Do I have to go anywhere? No. Every clue is solved on paper: in books, maps and records, many of them free online. The hunt never sends anyone onto private land or near a grave. I solved one. Now what? Post your answer in the comments on Facebook , with the book and page, or the link, where you found it. The first solver who can show the page is named in the next post and on the case board, and gets a solver’s keepsake to print. I’ve never done research before. Can I play? Yes. Every case page has a “Start here” box with the first pages to open, many of them free online. The glossary explains the old words, the guides show you how to read a death certificate and old handwriting , and the hunter’s worksheet keeps your notes straight. All you need is curiosity and, now and then, a library card. Can you help with my own family’s mystery? Yes. Write to research@projectscroll.com , or send Project Scroll a message on Facebook, with what you know. We’ll tell you honestly what the records are likely to show before you commit to anything. Can you write up my whole family’s history? Yes. We make family registers (every descendant of one couple), ancestral monographs (every ancestor of one person) and full family histories, built from the records with every statement marked. See a specimen , or download the sample family register . Do you also offer imaging, design, photography, 3D or video? Yes. Alongside the research, we scan and restore old photographs and documents, bring up faded ink, design family-history books and charts, photograph heirlooms and places, model landscapes in 3D from public LiDAR surveys, make 3D animations and family-history films, and keep living documents that grow with the research. See the studio work , then send us a message with what you have and what you would like made. What should I keep notes on? Use the hunter’s worksheet : one page to log each record, who made it, when, and where you found it. Print as many as you need. Is anything hidden on this website? Perhaps. There is a line of code at the foot of every page, a gold diamond that answers if asked, more than thirty tin badges to earn, and every page has a back side. Curious hunters know where to look. Who runs Project Scroll? An independent researcher and author who writes narrative nonfiction about the history of the Great Lakes country, trained in visual communications. The research behind those books is the same research we offer you, and the imaging and design studio grew from that training. More about Project Scroll . How is the hunt paid for? By sponsors: friends who give a few dollars a month, patrons who fund a case, local businesses with a card in the sponsors’ strip, and organizations that underwrite a hall. Sponsorship funds the work and never shapes a finding. How it works, and the ledger of what every gift paid for . How do I get in touch? Email research@projectscroll.com , or message the page on Facebook . Both reach the same desk. The form below lays out what to include. Expect a first reply within a few days; a full read of your records takes longer, and we say how long before we start. How long does a research case take? It depends on the question and on what survives. Some mysteries open in an afternoon; some take a season. After the first read we tell you what we expect to find, and roughly how long it should take, before you commit to anything. Does this website track me? Only if you say yes. On your first visit the site asks whether it may count your visit with a small Meta script; until you choose Allow, nothing is loaded and nothing is counted, and you can change your answer on the Privacy page. The things the site remembers, such as your followed cases and your notes, stay in you

← Research services Mysteries in the family Is the family story true? Every family has a story that has been told so often nobody questions it. Some are true. Some are half-true. Some began as a guess a hundred years ago. The records can usually tell which. Test a family legend Choose the story your family tells. Pick a story above to see what the records usually say about it, and how we would test yours. Tradition What families say. An inspector couldn’t spell it, so he wrote down something easier, and that became the family name. Document What the records usually show. Ellis Island inspectors did not write names down; they checked arrivals against passenger lists made at the port of departure. Names did change, often, but usually years later and by the family itself: at naturalization, at work, at school, or simply over time. How we test it Find the passenger list: it shows the name as written where the journey began. Find the naturalization papers, which often record both the old name and the new one. Follow the name census by census to see when the new spelling first appears. Reading The change almost always happened. Ellis Island almost never did it. Tradition What families say. A lord, a king, a governor or a famous founder sits at the top of the tree. Document What the records usually show. Some of these are true. Many began as a name match: someone of the right surname, in roughly the right place, adopted into the tree a century ago and copied forward until it looked like fact. How we test it Test the line one link at a time, starting with the most recent. Every parent–child joint needs its own record. Find who first printed the claim, and what they cited. Check the famous person’s documented children against the one the family claims. Reading Worth testing. Usually the line breaks at one particular joint, and finding it is a story in itself. Tradition What families say. A grandmother or great-grandmother was a Native princess, often said to be Cherokee. Document What the records usually show. The Cherokee Nation did not have princesses, and the story is so widespread that historians treat it as a family-legend pattern of its own. Some families do have Native ancestry, and the records that show it are specific: tribal rolls, agency censuses and treaty and allotment papers. How we test it Name the ancestor and place her in a census, with the people around her. Search the tribal rolls of the place and period (for the Cherokee: the Dawes and Guion Miller rolls, and the earlier rolls before them). A DNA test cannot show tribal membership; only the records and the nation itself can. Reading The princess is almost never real. The ancestor sometimes is, and deserves to be found properly. Tradition What families say. Three brothers arrived on one ship: one went north, one went south and one went west. Document What the records usually show. It is one of the most common stories in American family lore. Sometimes there were three brothers. Often there were three men of the same surname who were not related at all, later joined together to explain why the name turns up in different places. How we test it Find each man separately in the passenger lists, censuses and land records. Look for a document that names them as brothers: a will, a deed, a probate file. For male lines, a Y-DNA test can say whether their descendants share a father at all. Reading Often half-true: the men were real; the brotherhood is the part to test. Tradition What families say. Everything was lost in the fire, so there is no point looking. Document What the records usually show. Courthouses did burn, and records were lost. But deeds were often re-recorded afterward by the owners, and copies survive in state archives, churches, newspapers, tax rolls, military files and the records of neighboring counties. How we test it Find out exactly which years and which books were lost: it is rarely everything. Look for deeds re-recorded after the fire. Go around it: st

← Project Scroll Lost towns of the valley Towns that are not there any more Every county history has a page of places that were platted, named, given a mill or a store, and then left behind. Here are ten from the valley: why they were started, and what became of them. Most died the same way. A mill town grew up where a creek could turn a wheel; then the railroad came through somewhere else, trade followed the rails, and the mill was all that was left. Others never lived at all: paper towns drawn up in the land boom of 1836 and sold, or not sold, to people back East. Adamsport and Christiana (later Adamsville) Ontwa Township, Cass County, Michigan · on today’s map What was there. Two little plats faced each other across Christiana Creek: Christiana, laid out by Moses Sage, and Adamsport, laid out by Sterling Adams. The creek turned a grist mill, and a hotel followed. In 1882 the place had 133 people, a hotel, a blacksmith shop, a store and the mill. What happened. The two plats grew together under one name, Adamsville. When the railroads made new trading towns, it slipped back; by 1906 the mill was its only industry. “Both now are known by the name of Adamsville.” Rogers, 1875 The histories disagree on dates: Rogers puts Adamsport in September 1832 and Christiana in 1834; Mathews has March 1833 and May 1831. Williamsville Porter Township, Cass County, Michigan What was there. Josiah Williams laid it out in 1848 and had a hand in its first store. William R. Merritt’s store, opened in 1854, became “the trading place for miles around.” In 1882: two stores, two blacksmiths, a grist mill and a sawmill, one physician, 88 people. What happened. It simply never grew. “Its population has never reached much beyond the hundred mark.” Glover, 1906 Rogers says it was laid out in March 1848; Glover says the plat was filed on 5 July 1849. Kessington (also called Sailor) Mason Township, Cass County, Michigan What was there. Moses McKessick platted 19 lots on the Chicago road in 1872. In 1882 it had his general store, a blacksmith shop, a United Brethren church, a few houses and a schoolhouse. What happened. By 1906 the store and the smithy were gone. “one might drive over this site and notice nothing more remarkable at this country crossroads than a church and a school” Glover, 1906 Laid out 12 April 1872 (Rogers); the plat was recorded on 22 July (Mathews) or 23 July (Glover). Wakelee where four Cass County townships meet, Michigan · on today’s map What was there. Levi Garwood laid it out in 1871 on the new Peninsular railroad, later the Grand Trunk, and it was named for the line’s first treasurer, C. Wakelee. In 1882 it had 150 people, a store, a hotel, a blacksmith and a steam sawmill. What happened. It was a lumber station. When the timber was cut, the reason for it went too; it never incorporated, and its post office is long closed. “a large amount of lumber and wood is shipped from this point.” Mathews, 1882 Venice (a paper town) Wayne Township, Cass County, Michigan What was there. In August 1836, at the height of the land boom, Orlando Crane platted Venice on the South Dowagiac Creek: 538 lots and two public squares. What happened. Not one house was built and not one lot sold. The ground stayed farmland, and the city of Dowagiac later grew over it. “Nothing came of this attempt to boom the location; not a lot was sold” Glover, 1906 New Coloma Berrien County, Michigan What was there. In 1869, while the railroad was being finished, speculators laid out village lots by the line and gave ground for the station. Houses and stores went up. What happened. The stores closed for want of trade, buyers gave up their lots, and the speculators were left holding the buildings. “New Coloma became a barren reminder of promised greatness” History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties, 1880 Dennison, then Lowell across the river from South Bend, Indiana What was there. In 1837 the company that bought the east bank of the St. Joseph laid out a town opposite

Beckwith opened a foundry in Dowagiac in the 1850s and cast his first stove around 1867 to heat the struggling shop. ← The map room Cassopolis in LiDAR The county seat, laser by laser In 2015 an aircraft flew over Cass County firing laser pulses at the ground, hundreds of thousands a second, and timing each echo. Every dot below is one of those echoes: 355,650 of them, from the blocks around the courthouse. Turn it, tilt it, and lay the 1860 town plan over the real ground. Loading the survey… Drag to turn · scroll or pinch to zoom · right-drag or two fingers to move Buildings, 125,189 points Trees, 230,461 points The bare ground, with a contour every two metres What you are looking at Real survey points, not a drawing. Each dot is a laser return recorded by the U.S. Geological Survey’s 2015 flight over Cass County, placed to within a few centimetres. Roof shapes, chimneys and the crowns of single trees are all there because the laser hit them. The ground. The survey marks which returns struck bare earth. Those make the surface underneath, a model of the land with the buildings and trees taken off. It rises about 14 metres across these blocks. Buildings and trees. The survey does not say which of the other points are roofs and which are leaves, so we sorted them: a laser pulse that hits a roof comes back once; one that hits a tree comes back several times, from leaves, branches and the ground below. Flat, single echoes in a patch the size of a building are coloured gold. A few porches and dense evergreens may be the wrong colour. The 1860 plan. Press 1860 plan to lay the town plan from the 1860 county wall map on the ground. Its west part reaches into these blocks. Compare it with the flat then-and-now page . Height ×3. The town is fairly level, so tripling the heights makes the rise of the land easier to see. The buildings stretch too. Source: U.S. Geological Survey, 3D Elevation Program, Michigan Cass County LiDAR, 2015 (public domain), read from the survey’s public point-cloud archive. About one in two tree points is shown, to keep the page light; every building point is kept. The model covers the blocks north and east of the courthouse. x: ← The map room The valley in 3D The St. Joseph River Valley All 12,209 square kilometres that drain to the St. Joseph River, from the hills past Hillsdale to Lake Michigan, built from the U.S. Geological Survey’s laser-made elevation of the ground. The river and its branches are drawn in gold. Three lost towns are hidden in the hills: find all three. Height ×15 Loading the valley… Drag to turn · scroll or pinch to zoom · tap a gold light What you are looking at The whole watershed. The bright land is every acre whose rain ends in the St. Joseph River: parts of fifteen counties in Michigan and Indiana. The darker land around it drains elsewhere: to the Kalamazoo, the Maumee, the Kankakee, or straight to Lake Michigan. The shape of the ground. The heights come from the U.S. Geological Survey’s 3D Elevation Program, which in this country is made mostly from laser surveys flown county by county. Here it is sampled every 100 metres, and the heights are raised (×15 to start) because the valley falls only about 200 metres from its eastern hills to the lake. Use the slider to flatten it or raise it further. What the ice left. The long ridges and knobby hills are moraines, left where the glaciers stood and melted, about 15,000 years ago. The flat, open plains between them are outwash, sand and gravel spread by the meltwater. The river wanders through them both. The gold lights. Three are the sites of lost towns from the county histories. Tap each one. Find all three and the valley is yours: there is a badge for it. It is still there under another name. Fade to today and find what it is called now. Pearl Street at the south end of town. Today’s map spells it differently. The railroad crossing the north-east of town on its long diagonal, with the Depot Grounds and the passenger and freight depots. The race and Rock Run , the machine shop and the tannery beside them, and the Elkhart River on the west. The additions named for the men who laid them out: Barnes’s, Albright’s, Mayfield’s, Chamberlain’s and the rest. Each name is a lead to a plat in the county’s records. A challenge · Goshen Two streets that changed their names Market Street, on the south side of the Court House square, has a new name today, and Pearl Street at the south end of town is spelled another way. ← The map room Names on the old maps Who was in town Beside each town plan, the mapmakers printed a business directory: the lawyers, doctors, merchants, smiths, hotel keepers and county officers who paid to be listed. Here are 331 of those entries from five towns, with the 85 men of Company D, Sixth Michigan Infantry, raised at Dowagiac in 1861, as one roll you can search. Type a surname, a trade or a town. Search the roll 416 entries Elsewhere on the site Turn on JavaScript to search the roll. Each town’s directory can also be read on its plan in the map room . How to read the roll As printed. Names are spelled as the engraver cut them, abbreviations and all: Jas. for James, Wm. for William, Chas. for Charles. A spelling that looks wrong may be the engraver’s, or it may be how the family spelled it then. A question mark after a name means the engraving is worn or crowded and we are not sure of our reading. Look at the plan yourself and tell us what you see. Who is missing. A directory is not a census. It lists people who paid to appear, so most farmers, labourers, women and children are not here. A handful of entries are also held back because they would give away an answer in the hunt. Every entry links to its map. Open it and find the name in the directory beside the plan. Found someone of your own? A directory line is a start: it puts a person in a town, in a trade, in a year. Deeds, censuses, newspapers and probate files can take the story further. We can help. t: Band night at French’s Hotel, Eagle Lake
x: ← Front page · All the news Eagle Lake Band night at French’s Hotel, Eagle Lake A brass band on folding chairs under the trees, a flag strung overhead, and buggies and motor cars drawn up behind. A summer evening at Eagle Lake, on a card of 1912. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 2 min read Band concert, French’s Hotel, Eagle Lake, a real-photo postcard of 1912. Tinder Collection, Clements Library, University of Michigan. Edwardsburg, Mich. The band sits in a ring of folding chairs on the bare ground under the trees. The players wear peaked caps, their music is clipped to stands, and the trombones and the big bass drum stand out among the brass. A flag is strung on a line overhead. Around them the crowd stands close: men in shirtsleeves and straw hats, women in white, and in front one man grinning at the camera with a cigar in his teeth. Behind them are horses and a buggy, and motor cars with their tops up. Documented The words are written across the top of the card: “Band Concert, French’s Hotel, Eagle Lake, Mich.” It is a real-photo postcard of 1912, now in the David V. Tinder Collection at the University of Michigan. No photographer’s name appears on its face. French’s Documented Eagle Lake is in Ontwa Township, Edwardsburg’s own. The village’s history, as the Edwardsburg Chamber tells it, says that in summer “city folks detrained in the village” and were “driven by horse and carriage to French’s Resort on Eagle Lake.” The Edwardsburg Area History Museum has gathered the resort’s life in postcards, many of them provided by Floyd Jerdon of Dowagiac. Its gallery has French’s Landing about 1901 and in 1907, French’s Hotel in 1910 and 1911, another band concert at the resort in 1917, and “Hotel French’s, Eagle Lake Resort” still on a card of 1941. The Eagle Lake Sailing Club says it had its “early beginnings in 1936 at French’s Hotel.” Open questions Open Which band is this: Edwardsburg’s own, a band from Elkhart or South Bend, or the resort’s? Who was the French of French’s, when did the hotel open, and when did it close? Can you name anyone in the crowd? If you know, or if the band played in your family, write to research@projectscroll.com . The museum on Main Street in Edwardsburg is the place to see the rest of the cards. ← Front page · All the news Case 1 Who told Shepard? The only account of the 1846 lodge was written by a man who was a small child when it happened. Somebody told him. Who? Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 1 min read Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), p. 174, where the story is told again. Cassopolis, Mich. Everything we know about the lodge of 1846 comes from one account, written by James M. Shepard and printed in Rogers’s History of Cass County in 1875. Shepard did not see the lodge. He was a small child in 1846 and came to Cassopolis only in September 1868, as the village dentist. When he wrote, about 1875, three of the four charter men could still be found in or near the county: Dr. Evan J. Bonine at Niles, Jordan P. Osborn at Cassopolis, and Dr. Leander Osborn at Vandalia. And he was not sure of everything he had been told. In the 1875 text the founders are “the charter (?) members,” with his own question mark. Mathews, reprinting the passage in 1882, dropped it. So Case 1 asks: who told him? A founder, a member, a guest at the ball, the hotel’s keeper? The answer, if it survives, is in the record: in the books, the papers of the 1870s, or the lives of the men themselves. Case 1 was first opened on 15 October with a different question, whether the lodge ever had a real charter. That question answered itself in Shepard’s own question mark, so the case now asks the one beneath it. t: Company D: the 85 men Dowagiac sent in 1861
x: ← Front page · All the news Soldiers of the valley Company D: the 85 men Dowagiac sent in 1861 Raised at Dowagiac in the summer of 1861: who they were, where they fought, and the nineteen who did not come home. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 1 min read Monument Day, Dowagiac, on a real-photo postcard. Tinder Collection, Clements Library, University of Michigan. Dowagiac, Mich. In the summer of 1861 a company was raised at Dowagiac, the second organized in Cass County, under Captain Charles E. Clarke. It became Company D of the Sixth Michigan Infantry. The regiment gathered at Kalamazoo and left for the East on 30 August 1861, 944 strong. After garrison duty at Baltimore it went to New Orleans and the lower Mississippi, fought at Baton Rouge, and joined the assault on Port Hudson on 27 May 1863, where Lieutenant Frederick J. Clarke was killed. It ended the war as heavy artillery, and was discharged at Jackson, Michigan, on 5 September 1865. Of its men, four were killed or died of wounds and fifteen died of disease. As in the whole war, sickness killed more of them than battle did. The roll of all 85 men, as Mathews printed it in 1882, is now on the site, checked line by line against the page scans, with this week’s anniversaries from their service. ← Front page · All the news Old Cassopolis Dr. Goodwin’s hotel on Broadway A Civil War cavalry captain who became the village doctor built a hotel on Broadway and kept it himself. It took guests into the 1950s, and nothing of it is left. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 2 min read Hotel Goodwin, Cassopolis, Mich, 1916, C. R. Childs. David V. Tinder Collection of Michigan Photography, William L. Clements Library, University of Michigan. Cassopolis, Mich. Three storeys of brick under a mansard roof, with a pointed tower on the corner and HOTEL GOODWIN carved into the parapet. On the card of 1916 a covered wagon and two white horses wait at the kerb, there are striped awnings in the windows, and the last shop on the right has a sign that reads BAKERY. Documented The man behind the name was Dr. Fairfield Israel Goodwin. He served in the Civil War with Taylor’s Chicago Battery, was wounded at Iuka, and then raised Company C of the 8th Michigan Cavalry as its captain. He took his medical degree at the University of Michigan in 1874 and began to practise at Cassopolis the same year. The county history of 1906 says he was also active in real estate, and adds: “He built Hotel Goodwin and is its landlord.” He died in 1918. Reading A walking tour by the county and the Cass District Library’s Local History Branch says he built the hotel probably in 1896–97, in place of an earlier Goodwin hotel of 1887 at 130 South Broadway, a building that still stands. The tour says the Goodwin was a hotel until 1951 and was torn down in the late 1950s or early 1960s. A parking lot in front of Cassopolis Auto Supply is now on the site. Documented In the autumn of 1920 the hotel was badly damaged by fire, most of all inside. The South Bend News-Times called it “Cassopolis’ only hotel.” Two weeks later contractors had nearly finished the roof, and the proprietor, Carrie Ellis, planned to remodel and reopen within a month. Open In 1906 the county history placed the Goodwin House at the north edge of the old public square, on the west side of Broadway. The walking tour places the hotel near the southwest corner of Broadway and State. Which is right? And in what year did the first guest sign the register? Write to research@projectscroll.com . t: A lodge of E Clampus Vitus, in Cassopolis, in 1846
x: ← Front page · All the news E Clampus Vitus A lodge of E Clampus Vitus, in Cassopolis, in 1846 Two county histories record a lodge of the “Ancient and Honorable Order of Eclampsus Vitus” at Cassopolis, Michigan, in the spring of 1846: four charter members named, a ball of two hundred badges, and the earliest lodge of the order yet found with its members named. Newspapers of the same year show the order already at work across the state line in Indiana. Here is the whole record, what it does and does not prove, and the questions still open. By Michael Urbanski · Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 37 min read Rogers, History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 (1875), p. 253. Cassopolis, Mich. Picture a winter night in the county seat of a frontier county not yet twenty years old. The frame tavern on the square is lit up. Inside, more than two hundred people are wearing the badges of a secret society with a name few of them could have spelled the same way twice: the “Ancient and Honorable Order of Eclampsus Vitus.” It is the winter of 1846–47, and the Cassopolis lodge is less than a year old. In 1875 the first history of Cass County, Michigan, printed a short account of “the first Secret Society, of which there is any record” in the county: a lodge of the “Ancient and Honorable Order of the Eclampsus Vitus,” instituted at Cassopolis in the spring of 1846. Seven years later a second county history printed it again. Neither book was written for the order now known as E Clampus Vitus, and so far as we can find, no historian of that order has ever cited either one. A word to the Brethren If you wear the red shirt, you know the story: Ephraim Bee and his commission, Joe Zumwalt carrying the ritual to Hangtown, the lodge at Mokelumne Hill by 1851, and Carl Wheat bringing the order back to life in San Francisco in 1931. You also know the line in the order’s own 1966 history, that by 1849 “the East and Middle West were dotted with Clamper Lodges,” not one of them named. This page names one. It comes with a hall, a ball and four charter members, in the spring of 1846. And the newspapers of that year, just over the state line in Indiana, show the order alive and growing: a lodge at Connersville, a Tent No. 43 at Indianapolis meeting “in full regalia,” and a bill before the legislature to charter a lodge at Centreville. Credo quia absurdum , the motto runs: I believe because it is absurd. Here you will not need to. Every statement below is marked Documented (the record says so), Reading (our interpretation of it) or Open (not yet known), and every source is listed at the foot of the page. At a glance What A lodge of the “Ancient and Honorable Order of Eclampsus Vitus” Where Cassopolis, the county seat of Cass County, Michigan When Instituted in the spring of 1846; collapsed in 1847; revived in 1860 as “The Brothers of Charity” Charter members Dr. E. J. Bonine, Laban Harter, J. P. Osborn and Dr. L. Osborn; three of them married sisters of the Beall family The ball Winter of 1846–47, at the Union Hotel: “over two hundred badges” First printed Rogers, History of Cass County (1875), pp. 253–254, from an account by James M. Shepard Printed again Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), p. 174 Why it matters The earliest lodge of the order yet found with its members named, and the first known in Michigan. Indiana newspapers of 1846 confirm the order, and its spelling, in the same year New: E Clampus Vitus: the complete record . t: Edwardsburg in 1910, through J. Inbody’s camera
x: ← Front page · All the news Edwardsburg Edwardsburg in 1910, through J. Inbody’s camera A meat market and a bakery, a druggist selling ice cream soda next to the post office, and a frame school with a bell tower. Three cards by an Indiana photographer who made picture postcards. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 2 min read Elkhart St., Edwardsburg, Mich., a real-photo postcard of 1910, “Copr., Inbody.” Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Edwardsburg, Mich. About 1910 a photographer came to Edwardsburg and made three views of the village. Each card has its caption printed in white along the bottom, and each ends with the same two words: “Copr., Inbody.” All three are now at the Library of Congress. Documented Elkhart St. A row of frame stores with tin awnings. On the left, the window of a shop selling tobacco and cigars; next along, a sign for a MEAT MARKET and another for a BAKERY. A bicycle leans at the edge of the walk, a man stands under an awning, and a horse and wagon wait further down the street. Documented Post office. The village post office sits in a low frame building beside a brick corner store whose sign reads “B. C. Fisk, Druggist.” Its awnings advertise ICE CREAM SODA and CIGARS. Three people stand at the post office door, and on the fence to the left are show bills dated the 18th of June. The post office itself was old by then: the Chamber’s history says it was set up on 4 December 1828 as St. Joseph, renamed Edwardsburgh on 1 February 1830, closed for a time, restored on 23 August 1841, and lost its final “h” on a postmaster’s order in 1845. Reading Public school. A two-storey frame school with a pedimented front and a bell tower on the roof, standing in an open yard among young trees. The Chamber’s history says a two-storey frame school was built on the north side of Church Street in 1861, and a new brick school on Section Street in 1923. The card is probably the school of 1861, but we have not proved it. Our gallery has a second view of the same building, an Inbody card of 1911. Who was J. Inbody? Documented John Inbody, born 16 June 1866 and died 10 June 1915. On the back of his own portrait, taken about 1890 at A. J. Dawdy’s studio in Goshen, someone wrote: “He was a photographer, made picture postcards.” The Library of Congress catalogues one of his cards as published by “J. Inbody, Elkhart, Ind.” The site’s gallery holds his cards of Cassopolis, Edwardsburg, Elkhart, Goshen, Bristol and Pine Lake at La Porte, from 1909 to 1915. He worked the valley on both sides of the state line. Open Who kept the meat market and the bakery? What show was coming on 18 June? Zoom in on the cards: the smaller signs are there to be read. ← Front page · All the news How the towns got their names How Cassopolis got its name Everyone knows half of it: Cassopolis is the city of Cass. The other half is stranger. The county seat was first somewhere else, the man who won it for Stone Lake is said to have walked through a night of cold rain, and the village was spelled with an A for nearly forty years. By Michael Urbanski · Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 10 min read The plan of “Cassapolis” on Geil, Harley & Siverd’s Map of the Counties of Cass, Van Buren and Berrien (Philadelphia, 1860), detail. Library of Congress, Geography and Map Division. Cassopolis, Mich. Ask how Cassopolis got its name and the answer comes quickly: it is the city of Cass, named for Lewis Cass, governor of Michigan Territory, with the Greek word for a city on the end. That much is true. But the county seat was first at another village, the man who won it for Stone Lake is said to have walked through a night of cold rain to do it, and for nearly forty years the post office spelled the name with an A. We went back to the county’s three histories, of 1875, 1882 and 1906, to Michigan’s first gazetteer of 1838, and to the hand-coloured county map of 1860, to see what the record shows and what is only a good story. How to read this page Every statement below is marked Documented (a source says so, and you can read it), Reading (our interpretation of the sources) or Open (not yet known). Every source is listed at the foot of the page. At a glance The place Cassopolis, Michigan: the seat of Cass County, on the east shore of Stone Lake The county Named Cass by the act of the Legislative Council approved 29 October 1829 First county seat Not Cassopolis: Geneva, on Diamond Lake, chosen in 1830 The plat 1831: “a village to be called Cassapolis,” laid out by its proprietors on Stone Lake County seat By Acting Governor Mason’s proclamation, 19 December 1831 The spelling “Cassapolis” on the plat and at the post office until 1870; “Cassopolis” in print by 1838 Why it matters The name everyone can explain has a vowel nobody can; and the town got its name by winning the county seat The case in brief What the record shows The county was named Cass in 1829. The act says only “the name thereof shall be Cass.” That it honours Lewis Cass is understood, not written. The county seat came first to Geneva, on Diamond Lake, in 1830.
