Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Mishawaka, Ind. The card was made in 1910, and its captions do two jobs at once: “City Hall, Mishawaka, Ind.” and, under a portrait set into the sky, “Mayor Herzog.” The building was only six years old. The city had put it up in 1904 at First and Church Streets. Mishawaka was a young city, too. Its voters had turned the town into a city in 1899 and chosen Manuel Fisher as the first mayor. By the census of 1910 the city held 11,886 people, more than twice as many as in 1900. A new high school and St. Joseph Hospital both opened that year. The mayor Documented He was John A. Herzog, a Democrat, elected in November 1909; the papers printed his name in their lists of the new mayors across Indiana. Herzog was also State Chief Ranger of the Catholic Order of Foresters, and in July 1911 an Indiana paper introduced him as “State Chief Ranger John A. Herzog, mayor of Mishawaka.” The Foresters chose him again in June 1913. That autumn an earlier mayor, Melville W. Mix, ran again, and the South Bend News-Times said Mix would take up the work “continued along the same lines by Mayor Herzog.” In the election of November 1913 Mix lost by 423 votes to Ralph W. Gaylor, who ran as an independent. Where did it go? Open The South Bend Tribune wrote in 2022 that an older city hall on Church Street had stood where the police station is now, and that the city moved its offices to the old Bingham school in 1984. Today City Hall is at 100 Lincolnway West. Was the Church Street building the one on this card? When did it come down? If you know, write to research@projectscroll.com . t: Race day at the Cassopolis fair grounds
x: ← Front page · All the news Old Cassopolis Race day at the Cassopolis fair grounds A horse and sulky on the track, a crowd at the rail and a covered grandstand behind. Whose track was it, and where did the county fair run its races? Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 2 min read Race Track at Cassopolis, Mich., about 1905–1918. David V. Tinder Collection of Michigan Photography, William L. Clements Library, University of Michigan. Cassopolis, Mich. The card is a real photograph taken on the track itself. Men in hats and dark suits stand along the left. A horse in harness, hitched to a light sulky, is being led along the dirt. To the right is a raised judges’ stand, and beyond it a long line of people at the rail. Under the trees at the far end the dust hangs in the air. Documented The Cass County Agricultural Society was organised in the spring of 1851 and held its first fair that fall. According to the 1906 county history, its grounds had to move three times because of “the right of eminent domain.” Until 1857 the fairs were held on Samuel Graham’s land at Cassopolis. The railroads then took two sites in turn, and in 1871 the society bought twenty acres from Samuel Graham in the north part of the village for $3,000. After the 1884 fair a mortgage on the grounds was foreclosed, and the village of Cassopolis bought the land. In 1906 the village still owned it. Documented The society held no fairs after 1884. Then, in 1905, “a new organization was effected and held a successful fair.” The Billboard listed the Cassopolis fair for 22 to 25 September 1908. A harness-racing paper of 1916 records a horse that had started at Cassopolis in 1911. Documented The fair then stopped for three years. In October 1915 the South Bend News-Times reported that the Grangers had brought it back. Tents went up on the Cassopolis fair grounds again, the association got “the neglected race track” into shape, and the state master of the Grange spoke from the grandstand. Baseball and a motorcycle race came first, with horse races to follow on the Thursday and Friday. Open Was the track on this card the village’s twenty acres of 1871? Is any of it under today’s fairgrounds on North O’Keefe Street, where the Cass County Fair is still held? If you can place the grandstand, or you have a race programme from these years, write to research@projectscroll.com . See the old Cassopolis cards Can you place the grandstand? t: Springbrook Park, halfway between two cities
x: ← Front page · All the news Between two cities Springbrook Park, halfway between two cities For more than sixty years the park on the river between South Bend and Mishawaka gave the valley baseball, a summer theatre, band concerts and rides. Very little of it is left. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 2 min read Springbrook Park, South Bend, Ind. Postcard by The Indiana News Company, about 1910. St. Joseph County Public Library (South Bend, IN). South Bend, Ind. In 1901 a Walkerton paper put it in one line: Springbrook Park lay “midway between South Bend and Mishawaka.” It stood on the St. Joseph River, on what is now Lincolnway East. On the card a crowd in summer white walks along a pond, with a pavilion and the frame of a ride behind them. Documented Baseball came early. In June 1896 a team was to play all its games “on the new diamond at Springbrook Park,” and in 1897 the South Bend “Senators” played Whiting there. The railway’s park In June 1899 the papers reported that a vaudeville theatre would be built at the park, and in March 1901 that the railway company would put up a new summer theatre. By 1904 there were matinees at the Springbrook Park Casino. In April 1907, under the headline “White City for South Bend,” the Walkerton Independent reported that the Chicago, South Bend & Northern Indiana Railway, “which owns Springbrook park,” had leased it for ten years to the Interurban Amusement Company, which promised a big theatre, a dancing pavilion and other attractions. In the summer of 1914 there were Sunday band concerts, and families came out for picnic suppers. Playland Reading In the 1920s Earl J. “Pete” Redden took over the park and held a contest to rename it, and the winning name was Playland Park. The ballpark stayed. In the years after the Second World War the South Bend Blue Sox of the All-American Girls Professional Baseball League played their home games there. Open The park closed about 1960, and the land later became a golf course and then student housing for Indiana University South Bend. Pieces of the concrete grandstand are said to remain. Did you ride at Playland, or see the Blue Sox play? Do you know the year the gates closed for good? Write to research@projectscroll.com . t: Stone Lake, the lake that keeps secrets
x: ← Front page · All the news The lakes Stone Lake, the lake that keeps secrets No stream runs into Stone Lake, and none runs out. The village of Cassopolis was laid out on its shore in 1831, the county history of 1882 called it the most peculiar lake in the county, and people once believed it rose and fell with Lake Superior. Here is what the record says, and the seven mysteries it still keeps. By Michael Urbanski · Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 9 min read Stone Lake and the village on the Plan of Cassopolis in the Atlas of Cass County, Michigan (Philadelphia, 1872), detail. Internet Archive. Cassopolis, Mich. Stone Lake lies at the foot of Broadway in Cassopolis, close enough to the courthouse that the village was laid out around its shore. It is not large, and it is not famous. But it has puzzled people for a long time. No stream runs into it, and none runs out. Its water was soft when its neighbor’s was hard. And in the 1880s, by the county history’s account, many people in Cass County believed it was fed by an underground river from Lake Superior. We went back to the county histories of 1882 and 1906 and the county atlas of 1872 to see what the record says about the lake, and what it still keeps to itself. How to read this page Every statement below is marked Documented (a source says so, and you can read it), Reading (our interpretation of the sources) or Open (not yet known); a New finding is something we found in the record that we could not find in any earlier publication. Every source is listed at the foot of the page. At a glance The place Stone Lake, on the south side of the village of Cassopolis, the seat of Cass County, Michigan The name From the boulders: its shores “were originally very thickly strewn with stone, in the form of bowlders” (1882) Size 188 acres, in the county history’s table of 1882 The water “No visible inlet or outlet; its water is very fine and very soft,” while Diamond Lake’s, half a mile away, “is hard” (1882) The village Platted in 1831 beside the lake; the plat was “broken on the southwest corner by the lake” (1906) Drinking water From 1891 the village water works pumped from “the depths of Stone lake” (1906) Why it matters The lake shaped where the village grew, and it still keeps seven open questions The case in brief What the record shows The lake is named for its stones: boulders the glaciers left on its shores. It has no visible inlet or outlet, and its water was “very fine and very soft” in 1882, when Diamond Lake’s was hard. People believed in a river from Lake Superior. The 1882 history reports the belief that the lake was fed by “the great subterranean stream” from Superior, and rose and fell with it. The village was laid out on its shore, and for years drew its drinking water from it. What it does not show, yet Whether the lake still rises and falls when its neighbors don’t. Only people on the shore can tell us. Whether its water is still soft. A few dollars of test strips would answer it. Where the icehouse stood that, around 1899, supplied ice to the Diamond Lake cottages. Story or record? Play along Here are eight things people say about Stone Lake. For each, make your call: true, false, or no record either way. Then see what the paper shows. “The 1882 county history called Stone Lake the county’s most peculiar lake.” True “The largest is Diamond Lake … and the most peculiar is Stone Lake.” History of Cass County (1882), p. 11. “In 1882 Stone Lake’s water was hard, like Diamond Lake’s.” No Its water was “very fine and very soft”; Diamond Lake’s, “only half a mile distant, is hard.” 1882, p. 11. “Stone Lake is named for the boulders on its shores.” True Its shores “were originally very thickly strewn with stone, in the form of bowlders.” 1882, p. 11. “An underground river from Lake Superior feeds Stone Lake.” No record The 1882 history says only that it was “supposed by many people.” No study has ever shown it. “Cassopolis once drank Stone Lake water.” True From 1891 the wat

t: Summer on Diamond Lake: Forest Hall and the island
x: ← Front page · All the news Diamond Lake Summer on Diamond Lake: Forest Hall and the island A tennis net on the lawn, a windmill over the roof and the name along the ridge: Forest Hall, 1909. Across the water, a hotel on an island, with a cannon on its grass. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 3 min read Forest Hall, Diamond Lake, Cassopolis, a real-photo postcard of 1909 published by O. L. Yerty, Cassopolis. Tinder Collection, Clements Library, University of Michigan. Cassopolis, Mich. A tennis net is stretched across the lawn. Players stand at the net with their rackets, others watch from the shade, and a windmill stands above the roof. Along the ridge, in big letters, is the name: FOREST HALL. The card was published in 1909 by O. L. Yerty of Cassopolis, and the caption on its face reads “Forest Hall – Diamond Lake.” What Forest Hall was Reading The Diamond Lake Association keeps a timeline of the lake, compiled by Jean Schultz from local sources and crediting Lois Webster Welch’s book A Diamond Sparkles . It says the house began in 1872 as “The Chicago House,” a vacation home on the north shore built by three officials of the Michigan Central Railroad. In 1880 it was renamed Forest Hall and leased as a public resort, and in 1891 a Mr. Rudd and a Dr. Laughton bought it and made it a health resort. A nine-hole golf course was laid out on its grounds in 1921. Forest Hall closed as a resort hotel in 1926 but stayed on as the clubhouse of the Diamond Lake Golf Club, and in 1935 it was torn down and its wood used to build a new clubhouse. Documented The county history of 1906 bears out the date of 1891. In the life of the hotel’s proprietor, Glover writes: “In 1891 he purchased the Forest Hall Hotel, which he has since been conducting.” He adds that the hotel had become “a favorite summer resort.” Forest Hall was not alone. The association’s timeline counts five resort hotels on the lake by 1900, and Glover describes another of them, Shore Acres, as “an attractive summer hotel.” The island Documented The island was known long before the hotels. Mathews, in 1882, gives Diamond Lake an area of 1,083 acres, and he gives a section of his book to Job Wright, “the recluse of Diamond Lake Island,” and tells of Wright’s prediction of “Harrison’s early death.” The association’s timeline says Wright built a log cabin on the island in 1829 and lived there until he died in 1842. Reading Then the summer crowds came. By the association’s timeline, picnic parties were going over to the island in 1873. In 1878 Fred Moon and Colonel Allen built a croquet court, a roller skating rink, an outdoor dance platform and an amphitheater there, and the Cassopolis Vigilant reported in 1879 that there were now enough buildings on the island “to shelter 5000 people from storms.” In 1889 Captain John Bartlett bought the island and took over the Diamond Lake Island Hotel. The hotel closed in 1919, and in 1925 the island was platted for sale as residential lots. Open One postcard in the strip at the top of this site is captioned “The Island House, Diamond Lake, Cassopolis”: a long frame building with a deep porch, young trees along the path, and a field gun on its wheels on the lawn. Was the Island House the same building as the Diamond Lake Island Hotel? Was that the gun fired on the Fourth of July in 1882, when the timeline says the island celebrated “by shooting off fireworks and artillery”? And who was the proprietor Glover wrote about? His life begins on page 755 of Glover. If you know, or have a card or a photograph, write to research@projectscroll.com . ← Front page · All the news The Underground Railroad The Bonine House at Vandalia A Quaker family from Indiana, a farm of 1,600 acres, an elk park that answered to its owner’s call and sent elk to the King of Italy, and a house now kept by the Underground Railroad Society of Cass County. What the record says about the James E. Bonine House, and what it has yet to show. By Michael Urbanski · Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 19 min read James E. Bonine’s farm as the county history described it in 1882: History of Cass County, Michigan (Chicago, 1882), p. 251. Internet Archive. New finding What’s new here The earliest description we have found of the building now called the Bonine carriage house: in 1882, “exactly opposite his residence, which is on a corner,” “the finely-built storehouse,” with two rows of arbor vitae running from it. The history says nothing of fugitives there. Found by Michael Urbanski, Project Scroll, 22 October 2026. What we searched The Underground Railroad Society of Cass County’s pages on the house and carriage house; eight Leader articles of 2009–2021; the Clio entries; local radio and television features; Wikipedia; web searches for Bonine with “storehouse” and “arbor vitae”. The Bonine named in Wilbur Siebert’s national directory of Underground Railroad workers (1898) is Isaac, the father: “Bogue, Steven. Bonine, Isaac. Shugart, Zachariah.” Modern accounts credit his son James E., and none we have found cites Siebert. Found by Michael Urbanski, Project Scroll, 22 October 2026. What we searched The same sources as for the storehouse, with web searches for Siebert with “Isaac Bonine”. Glover’s history of 1906 places the meeting of the Anti-Slavery Friends of Cass County, with the Rev. Charles Osborn as pastor, “in a log building in the grove on the farm of the late James E. Bonine … known as the Elk Park.” Modern accounts say only that the Bonines were members. Found by Michael Urbanski, Project Scroll, 22 October 2026. What we searched The same sources as for the storehouse, with web searches for the Anti-Slavery Friends with Bonine and Elk Park. The earliest eyewitness account of the Bonine elk park, in the Michigan Farmer of 18 August 1885, says two elk “went to Victor Emanual, the King of Italy, … to grace the Royal Park,” with no warship, against the seven elk and “war vessel” of the 1882 county history. The same visitor describes a 40-acre park behind a ten-foot fence, ten elk and thirteen deer, the elk coming to the call “Come Bill!”, and a large fountain and flagstone walks before the house. Found by Michael Urbanski, Project Scroll, 22 October 2026. What we searched The Underground Railroad Society of Cass County’s pages on the house, carriage house and Quaker timeline; eight Leader articles of 2009–2021; the Clio entry; local radio and television features; Wikipedia; Internet Archive full-text searches for Bonine with elk, Italy and “Victor Emmanuel”; Italian sources on the wapiti of La Mandria, none of which names Michigan. The Bonine Elk Park outlived its founder by half a century. Isaac A. Bonine wrote to the federal Biological Survey in 1907 that he had bred elk “for about thirty-five years”; a 1908 newspaper reports elk sold at $100 a head to parks in Detroit and Grand Rapids; and in October 1953 a newspaper photograph shows “a herd of 12 to 15 elk at Bonine Elk Park” on M-60, still owned by the founder’s great-grandson. Found by Michael Urbanski, Project Scroll, 22 October 2026. t: The courthouse that became the Colonial
x: ← Front page · All the news Old Cassopolis The courthouse that became the Colonial The Colonial Opera House on a card of 1913 had served Cass County as its courthouse for more than half a century before it was moved across the village. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 1 min read The Colonial Opera House, Cassopolis, Mich., 1913. David V. Tinder Collection of Michigan Photography, William L. Clements Library, University of Michigan. Cassopolis, Mich. A white frame building with tall columns, a pediment and a domed cupola. Across the front, in capitals: THE COLONIAL. The caption, written across the foot of the card, reads “Colonial Opera House, Cassopolis, Mich.” The card dates from 1913. Documented The building was older than it looks. It was the county’s second courthouse, a two-storey frame building finished in 1841, and for more than half a century it stood on the northeast quarter of the public square. When the stone courthouse replaced it, it was sold and moved to the south side of State Street, west of Broadway. In 1906 the county history found it there “used as a storage house.” Documented By the time of the card it was a place of entertainment. In April 1917 the high school chorus gave a comic operetta at “the Colonial theater.” The Film Daily Year Book of 1927 lists the Colonial at Cassopolis with 476 seats. It was remodelled in 1937 as the Gem Theatre, showed films until 1960, and was torn down in 1968. Open When did the old courthouse become an opera house? A theatre history says it opened as the Colonial Opera House in 1899, with 420 seats, and became the Colonial Theatre in 1909. But the county history of 1906 calls it a storage house. And where did the name come from? In 1906 the historian wrote that its lines combined “the Greek temple with Colonial residences.” If you have a programme, a ticket or a diary entry that settles it, write to research@projectscroll.com . t: The day 3,000 people came to watch one log
x: ← Front page · All the news From 1923 The day 3,000 people came to watch one log Twenty-four men carried the first log of the Pioneer Log Cabin while a band played. Four weeks later the cabin was finished. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 1 min read The card of 1923, Building the Pioneer Log Cabin. Private collection. Cassopolis, Mich. At half past eight on the morning of 23 May 1923, a black walnut log twenty-six feet long was carried to its place by twenty-four men. A band played and the crowd sang. About three thousand people stood and watched, and many had driven up to fifty miles to be there. It was the first log of the Cass County Pioneer Log Cabin. A note written on the back of one card of the day says fifty-two volunteers did the first morning’s work. The logs came from families across the county, given from their own land. Each log was numbered, and a list kept the family’s name, the town and the kind of tree. The card printed for the occasion gives the whole job in one line: May 23 to June 20, 1923. Four weeks, from the first log to Pioneer Day. The cabin still stands in Cassopolis today, as the Pioneer Log Cabin Museum. x: ← Front page · All the news In season The harvest trail: a mill, an orchard and the stove town Stamp three places in your passport this fall, from September to November, and earn the harvest badge. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 1 min read An orchard at its best, near Benton Harbor and St. Joseph, about 1930 to 1945. Boston Public Library, Tichnor Brothers Collection. The St. Joseph River valley. Fall is harvest time in the valley, and the passport has a trail just for it. The mill. Bonneyville Mill near Bristol, Indiana, a county park around a historic grist mill that still grinds flour, open Tuesday to Sunday until mid-November. The orchard. Jollay Orchards near Coloma, where the same family has farmed since 1857: u-pick fruit, fresh cider and apple-cinnamon doughnuts. The stove town. The Dowagiac Area History Museum, free, where the story of the Round Oak Stove Company is told. Press “I’m here” at all three between September and November of the same year, and the harvest badge is yours. Check each place’s hours before you go. ← Front page · All the news Case 2 The hotel that walked away In 1867 the old hotel where the lodge held its ball was hauled across Cassopolis and turned into a mill. Where did it end up? Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 1 min read The hotel’s block on the 1860 Geil, Harley & Siverd wall map. Library of Congress. Cassopolis, Mich. The old hotel stood at the northwest corner of Broadway and State Street, at the heart of the village. It was the Union Hotel, where the lodge of 1846 held its grand ball. In 1852 the Masons held their first meeting under the same roof, and on the 1860 wall map of the county the engraver cut one word on its block: HOTEL. Then, in 1867, the building was hauled across the village and turned into a mill, and a new hotel rose on its ground. Where did the old hotel end up, and is any of it still standing? That is Case 2 on the board. The first sources are the county histories of 1882 and 1906, free to read online. ← Front page · All the news The Underground Railroad The Kentucky Raid of 1847 In the summer of 1847 a party of Kentuckians came to the Quaker farms of Cass County to carry nine people back into slavery. Their neighbors stopped them at O’Dell’s mill, a hearing at Cassopolis set the nine free, and the lawsuits ran on for five years. We went back to the papers of 1847, the court files and the county histories. By Michael Urbanski · Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 12 min read The chapter heading in Howard S. Rogers, History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 (Cassopolis, 1875), p. 131. Internet Archive. New finding What’s new here The raiders’ own home paper, the Covington Licking Valley Register of 17 September 1847, put their bail at “something over four thousand dollars.” Every later account we have found gives $2,600, the 1882 county history’s figure. Found by Michael Urbanski, Project Scroll, 22 October 2026. What we searched The county histories of 1875, 1882 and 1906; the House Divided project’s narrative of the 1847 stampedes; D. G. Chardavoyne’s article in The Court Legacy (2004); Wikipedia; the Underground Railroad Society of Cass County’s pages; the Clio entry; the State Bar of Michigan’s milestone pages; web searches for the bail figure. The same 1847 Kentucky account says the raiders’ baggage wagon, its wheels taken, “was then delivered up.” The earliest telling we know of the story that it was rolled into Birch Lake is in newspapers of 1936–37, and no account we have found sets the two side by side. Found by Michael Urbanski, Project Scroll, 22 October 2026. What we searched The county histories of 1875 and 1882, searched for “wagon”; the House Divided narrative; Wikipedia; the society’s pages; web searches for the wagon and Birch Lake. A new finding is a fact found in a primary source that we could not find in any published history, article or website we searched. Credit: Michael Urbanski, Project Scroll. If you know of an earlier publication, tell us and we will say so here. All our discoveries › Cassopolis, Mich. In the summer of 1847 a party of Kentuckians rode into Cass County to take back people who had escaped from slavery and were living and working on the Quaker farms around Young’s Prairie. In one night they seized nine. By the next morning the neighbors had caught up with them near O’Dell’s mill, at what is now Vandalia, and a crowd of several hundred walked raiders and captives together to Cassopolis. There a county commissioner heard the case and set the nine free, and that same day a party of fifty-two started north for Canada. The story is told every year in Cass County, and some of what is told has grown in the telling. We went back to what was written at the time: the Covington, Kentucky, newspaper that spoke for the raiders, the federal court papers, a freedom seeker’s own account, and the county histories of 1875, 1882 and 1906. Every source is listed at the foot of the page. t: The Newton House, a farmhouse museum near Decatur
x: ← Front page · All the news Near Decatur The Newton House, a farmhouse museum near Decatur One family lived in this Volinia Township house from 1844 to 1930. Today it is a museum, open on the first Sunday of each month from June to September. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 2 min read Map of the Counties of Cass, Van Buren and Berrien, Michigan, published by Geil, Harley & Siverd, Philadelphia, 1860. Library of Congress. Volinia Township, Mich. On the 1860 wall map of Cass, Van Buren and Berrien counties, Volinia is the third township along the top row of Cass County. Directly above it, across the heavy county line, is Decatur Township in Van Buren County, and the plan of Decatur village is one of the small insets on the map’s left side. In Volinia, on the Marcellus Highway, stands the Newton House. The house Documented By the Cass County Historical Society’s account, the house was “built by Colonel James Newton in 1844.” In 1868 his son George Newton “commissioned the architect Christian Haefner to design and build an addition,” and the house is “a fine example of nineteenth century Italianate architecture.” The family lived in it until 1930. The state marker on the road, put up in 1977, puts it more briefly: “Designed by Christian Haefner in the 1860s, this house belonged to George Newton, a state legislator.” Documented Rogers’s county history of 1875 has the Newtons’ lives. Colonel James Newton was born in England in 1777, came to America as a boy and moved to Ohio in 1804. George was born in Preble County, Ohio, in 1810 and came to Michigan with his father in 1831. George taught the first school in the Higgins schoolhouse, the winter after it was built in 1836, and in 1858 he was elected to the state legislature. Documented In 1931 Fred Russ bought the house and the timberland around it, and in 1942 the land went to Michigan State University as a gift. It became the Fred Russ Experimental Forest, 580 acres, and the house was restored by the Cass County Historical Commission. A 40-acre stand of oak and hickory in the forest, named Newton Woods after George Newton, was made a National Natural Landmark in 1976. The house was entered on the state register of historic sites in 1974 and on the National Register of Historic Places in 1982. Visiting The Newton House is at 20689 Marcellus Highway, Decatur, and opens its doors on the first Sunday of each month from June to September, 1:00 to 4:30 pm. The 2026 season is over; check the society’s website before you go next summer. Its rooms show daily life across the years the Newtons lived there, and several are set aside for reading and research on the family, the woods around the house and local history. The county has leased the house from the university since 1980; in June 2026 the university’s trustees agreed to sell it to the historical society, and we have not yet been able to confirm that the sale has closed. One more thing to try: open the 1860 map, find Volinia, and see whether the Newton name is on its farms. The Newton House, hours and directions Volinia on the 1860 map Found the Newtons on the map? t: The night 3,000 were invited to the Oliver Hotel
x: ← Front page · All the news South Bend The night 3,000 were invited to the Oliver Hotel James Oliver, the plow maker, built South Bend a grand hotel at Main and Washington. It opened the week before Christmas 1899 and stood until 1967. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 2 min read Oliver Hotel, South Bend, Indiana. Postcard by the E. C. Kropp Co., Milwaukee, before 1917. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. South Bend, Ind. On the evening of 20 December 1899 the new Oliver Hotel held its first reception. About three thousand invitations had gone out, to South Bend, Chicago and other cities. Palms and cut flowers filled the rooms, a buffet supper was served all evening, and every part of the house was open for guests to look over. The next day it opened to the public. The host was James Oliver, the South Bend plow maker. With him stood his wife, his son Joseph D. Oliver and his wife, and his only daughter and her husband, George Ford. The Indianapolis Journal ’s man in South Bend called it “probably the largest” reception ever given in the city. Built for the plow trade Customers of the plow works came to South Bend from overseas, and until then, the History Museum says, there was nowhere fit to put them up. So the Olivers built a hotel themselves. The first stone of the foundation was laid in July 1898 at the northwest corner of Main and Washington Streets, and James Oliver, then in his seventies, watched over most of the work. The hotel had 250 guest rooms, and its first manager was Charles Baur, who had come from Terre Haute. It made its own electricity, with three dynamos to light 1,700 lamps. The lobby and rotunda were done in the Italian Renaissance style and trimmed with gold, and sixteen painted women at the top of the rotunda stood for the seasons, the arts and the four elements. The South Bend Tribune called it “the most magnificent hotel in Indiana.” What became of it In later years it was the Pick-Oliver. Its big sign was taken down in November 1957, and in the late summer of 1967 the wrecking ball brought the building down while people on the sidewalk watched. A bank tower went up on the corner, and it is now the Chase Tower. Open Did you stay at the Oliver, or eat in its dining room? Do you have a menu, a key or a piece of its china? t: Five minutes with Roosevelt at Dowagiac
x: ← Front page · All the news Dowagiac, 1912 Five minutes with Roosevelt at Dowagiac On Saturday, 30 March 1912, Theodore Roosevelt’s train stopped at Dowagiac on its way across Michigan. Oscar C. Haight’s camera caught the crowd. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 2 min read Roosevelt Special, March 30th 1912. Real-photo postcard by Oscar C. Haight. David V. Tinder Collection of Michigan Photography, William L. Clements Library, University of Michigan. Dowagiac, Mich. The news came the day before. As the Dowagiac museum’s Steve Arseneau retold it in 2016 from the Dowagiac Daily News , the paper called it an “exclusive announcement”: the former president would halt his special train in Dowagiac “and make a five minute speech from the rear platform.” Few people in the town had ever seen him. It was Saturday, 30 March 1912, and Roosevelt was campaigning to take the Republican nomination from President Taft. The stores were to close for the visit. A whistle at the water works was to sound when the train left Niles, and the interurban from Benton Harbor and St. Joseph ran a special schedule to bring people in from Berrien County. Late, and brief The train had left Chicago late and came in about an hour behind time, at half past three. Roosevelt began, as the paper reported it, “Ladies, gentlemen and babies,” and spoke for about five minutes, mostly about a bill to give Michigan a primary election. He wished he could stay longer, the paper said, but all he could say was “good luck and good bye.” The Daily News headline read “Monster Crowd Sees Roosevelt: Colonel Talks For 5 Minutes.” Twelve hours in Michigan Documented Dowagiac was one stop on a long day. A wire story printed in Michigan papers the next week said the colonel put in “12 strenuous hours” in the state, with speeches from the car platform at Kalamazoo, Battle Creek and Ann Arbor. That night he spoke for an hour at the Light Guard armory in Detroit. The hall was full an hour early, about a thousand people waited in the street, and it was announced from the stage that he would speak to them from a balcony of the Hotel Cadillac. Haight’s card, signed “Haight Photo.”, shows the crowd packed across the tracks by the depot, with the train at the right. Open Is your family in that crowd? ← Front page · All the news Made in the Valley Stoves, lures, wagons and guitars Twenty-three makers from the valley: what they made, how they ended, and where you can still see their work. Project Scroll · 21 October 2026 · 1 min read New Round Oak Warehouse, Dowagiac, about 1910 to 1918. Tinder Collection, Clements Library, University of Michigan. The St. Joseph River valley. For a century the towns of the valley made things the whole country knew by name. Round Oak stoves came out of Dowagiac from 1871. James Heddon’s Sons made fishing lures there from 1902. Studebaker built wagons in South Bend, then cars. Gibson made mandolins and guitars in Kalamazoo, and C. G. Conn made band instruments in Elkhart. The new Made in the Valley page follows twenty-three of them: who founded each one, what it made, when it peaked, how it ended, and the museums where its work is still on show. Every maker is pinned on a map, and set on a timeline that runs from the 1850s to today. t: Where Kellogg made its telephone cabinets
x: ← Front page · All the news Old Cassopolis Where Kellogg made its telephone cabinets For years the oak cases of Kellogg telephones and switchboards were made in Cassopolis. An old postcard shows the plant, the lumber stacked by the railroad, and the words “Cabinet Shops” painted on the wall. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 2 min read Kellogg Switchboard & Supply Co, Cassopolis, Mich., about 1908–1916, published by O. L. Yerty, Cassopolis. David V. Tinder Collection of Michigan Photography, William L. Clements Library, University of Michigan. Cassopolis, Mich. The card is a real photograph. Long stacks of sawn boards lie in the grass in front, a flatcar stands on the siding, and behind the tracks rise the long, many-windowed buildings of the Kellogg Switchboard & Supply Co. A chimney smokes. On the nearest wall, if you look closely, are the words “Cabinet Shops.” Documented The company was a Chicago maker of telephones and switchboards, founded in 1897. In August 1906 a Paw Paw newspaper reported that Kellogg would put its new woodworking department in Cassopolis. The citizens of the village were to turn over the land and buildings of the late Cassopolis Drill Co., and the title would pass to Kellogg once it had spent an agreed sum on labour and additions. Documented The plant grew. In 1909 the trade journal Telephony counted seven buildings with 46,000 square feet. In November 1910 the company filed papers at Lansing for its Cassopolis woodworking plant and said it had a $75,000 plant there, where “the cabinet work for Kellogg switchboards and telephones” was made. By 1915 there were eight buildings, two warehouses and a dry kiln. Documented In April 1917 the South Bend News-Times reported seventy men at work and six more wanted. There were orders from Italy, from the Dutch East Indies and from the Russian government, and some departments worked until nine at night. That August Telephony walked its readers through an eight-acre plant with a two-acre lumber yard, where tiers of oak waited for the kiln and a new building was going up. Reading The work did not stop with the war. A Kellogg advertising budget printed in Printers’ Ink in 1929 still lists taxes for “Chicago & Cassopolis.” Open When did the Cassopolis plant close, and what stands on its ground today? Where exactly were the old drill works? If you know, or if you have a Kellogg telephone with a Cassopolis case, write to research@projectscroll.com . ← Front page · All the news Names on the old maps Who was in town in 1860? 331 names from the business directories printed beside the old town plans, with the men of Company D, in one roll you can search. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 1 min read The Cassopolis directory beside the village plan, 1860 wall map. Library of Congress. The St. Joseph River valley. Beside each town plan on the old county maps, the mapmakers printed a business directory: the lawyers, doctors, merchants, smiths, hotel keepers and county officers who paid to be listed. Now 331 of those entries, from Cassopolis, Dowagiac, Niles and Paw Paw in 1860 and Goshen in 1861, are in one roll you can search by surname, trade or town, together with the 85 men of Company D. A directory is not a census. It lists the people who paid to appear, so most farmers, labourers, women and children are not in it. But a directory line puts a person in a town, in a trade, in a year, and that is often the first step to finding a family. ← Project Scroll Newspaper of the month The True Northerner, 1 February 1899 One page of an old valley paper, read slowly. This month: the back page of Paw Paw’s weekly, in the middle of a Michigan winter, with egg prices, a farmers’ meeting and the war with Spain at the opera house. The True Northerner was the weekly of Paw Paw, the seat of Van Buren County. Its back page that week was a working page: the market report, the end of a long account of a farmers’ institute, the circuit court, real-estate sales, and the advertisements that paid for it all. Tap any clipping to see it at full size, or open the whole page at the Library of Congress. Our local markets This is what Paw Paw dealers paid farmers that week, not what the shops charged. Butter 12 cents (a pound), eggs 14 cents (a dozen), potatoes 25 cents and wheat 65 cents (a bushel). The units were so well known that the paper did not print them. Cattle and hogs were priced by the pound, “on foot” (alive) or dressed. Above the list, the corner of an advertisement for Royal Baking Powder: “Absolutely Pure,” seven years before the Pure Food and Drug Act. The farmers vote A winter farmers’ institute in Van Buren County passed these resolutions. Senators “should be elected by the people”: in 1899 state legislatures still chose them, and the Seventeenth Amendment did not change that until 1913. County officers should draw a salary instead of keeping fees. And fruit should carry “the name and address of the shipper,” an early demand for honest labels from the fruit belt. A dollar a bushel A. S. Packard of Covert, “one of the most successful peach growers in the county,” told the institute that his last crop came to about 3,000 bushels and averaged him over a dollar a bushel. Peaches were the money crop of the Michigan fruit belt, and the paper promised to print his paper in full. At what age should a child read? The evening session argued about schools. The institute’s president thought a child should be in the second reader by five or six “if it were not for the laziness of parents.” Alice Bangs disagreed: no child ought to begin before six. The paper calls her Miss in one line and Mrs. in the next; the rest of the report says the audience nodded with her. The war at the opera house Six months after the fighting with Spain ended, a travelling company brought moving pictures of it to Longwell’s opera house for one night, Saturday, 4 February. The Lumière cinématographe had been shown for the first time only four years before. Many “war films” of the day were staged re-enactments, so the audience could not always tell what was real. Admission was 10 and 20 cents. Every soldier, life size The advertisement across the foot of the page made the real promise: the reviews of the Michigan volunteer regiments would show “every soldier from Paw Paw and vicinity life size so that each and every one can readily be recognized.” Another notice on the page says that at Grand Rapids parents saw sons who had since been buried in Cuba. Saw edges Men wore detachable starched collars, and a badly ironed one left a rough edge that cut the neck. The Model Steam Laundry on South Kalamazoo Street claimed to be the only laundry in southern Michigan that could take the “saw edges” off. Read the page yourself What did a Paw Paw dealer pay for a dozen eggs? 14 cents. Who chose United States senators in 1899? The state legislatures. Direct election came with the Seventeenth Amendment in 1913. How many bushels of peaches did Mr. Packard grow? About 3,000, at over a dollar a bushel. What was showing at Longwell’s opera house on 4 February? Moving pictures of the Spanish-American War, by a Lumière cinématographe company. Reading an old paper Start with the ads and the markets. They tell you what things cost, who kept which shop, and what people wanted to buy. Read the “continued from” stories. The front page opens a story; the back page often holds the names. Do not trust the typed text. The searchable text

← The places Berrien County, Michigan Niles, Michigan: its history, in the record Niles stands on the St. Joseph River beside the site of Fort St. Joseph: a Jesuit mission of 1691 and a French fort of 1697, and four flags have flown there — French, British, Spanish and American — which is why the city calls itself the City of Four Flags. The present town was settled in 1827 and named for Hezekiah Niles, the Baltimore newspaper editor. The town at a glance Founded: the mission 1691, the fort 1697; the town settled 1827; village 1835; city 1859. Name: for Hezekiah Niles (1777–1839), editor of Niles’ Weekly Register. In the record: the Fort St. Joseph archaeological project of Western Michigan University; Ellis’s history of Berrien and Van Buren counties (1880) and Coolidge’s of Berrien (1906); the Niles Republican and Niles Democrat. On the map: the 1860 Geil & Harley county map’s Niles inset shows the river through the plan; lay it over today’s streets . The hunt: Niles is the first town outside Cass County in the hunt, and the river road to it runs through the early cases. On old postcards Niles, Berrien County, Michigan (bird's-eye view) · 1868, A. Ruger; Chicago Lithographing Co. Library of Congress, Geography and Map Division · source Main St., Niles, Mich. · about 1905–1915 Private collection; scan shared online From public-domain postcards and photographs, each linked to the library that holds it. See them all . Where to look Niles holds the oldest written record in the valley, the Fort St. Joseph registers and the fur-trade accounts, and the best run of nineteenth-century newspapers in the two counties. For families on the Berrien side of the line, start here. The records page links each source where it is held, and the glossary explains the words the old records use. ← All field notes Field notes · No. 1 · 17 October 2026 One Letter, Two Certificates One letter. That’s all it was. A single middle initial, and it nearly turned one man into two. The case A pioneer died in Michigan in 1912. The old county histories give him a plain first and last name. One of them adds “Senior.” County history His own death certificate, filed about a month after he died, gives the same plain name. No initial at all. Document Then we found his son’s death certificate, from 1935. In the box for the father’s name, whoever answered the questions gave him a middle initial: the same one the son carried. Document So which is right? Make your guess now. Ours is further down. Then it got stranger Once we started comparing every box, the records kept arguing. His birthday: his death certificate and one of the county histories are two days apart. His father’s birthplace: the certificate names one state. That same history names another. One man, one family and three disagreements. Nobody lied. Each one is somebody’s memory. What this teaches Every record was written by someone. A death certificate tells you what the informant believed, on a hard day. Their name is usually on it. The father’s was filed about a month after he died; the son’s was filled in twenty-three years later, by someone remembering a man long gone. County histories have the same weakness: the family usually supplied the facts, often from memory, and nobody checked them. One letter can change everything. Fathers and sons with the same name get tangled in the record all the time. One wrong initial can merge two men or split one, and send you chasing somebody else’s family for a month. Watch out for “Senior.” In the 1800s it didn’t always mean “father.” Sometimes it only meant the older of two men with the same name in town, related or not. Here a son with the same name does turn up, so the label fits, but always check. Disagreement is a clue, not a failure. Every mismatch tells you who was remembering, and when. Our guess, as promised: father and son shared a name, and in 1935 someone gave the father the son’s initial too Reading . But a guess is not proof. Four rules for when records disagree Ask who gave the information, and when. Closer to the event usually weighs more, but not always. Keep looking. A third, independent record can tip the balance, but records are weighed, not counted. Write down both versions and where each came from. Never quietly “fix” one. Call it settled only when the evidence settles it. Until then, it’s an open question. Where the case stands Open Our next witness: a local newspaper notice from the days or weeks after his death. Then his probate file, and the cemetery’s burial records or a transcription of his stone. Read the stone on paper. Don’t go to it. Marks, strongest first: Document Period print County history Compiled Tradition Field (seen at first hand) Inference Reading Hypothesis — what the marks mean Where to look, for free Archives of Michigan, death certificates 1897–1952 . Free; for most years you can open the certificate itself, in the original handwriting. FamilySearch . Birth, marriage and death records from all over the world, free with an account. Michiganology: vital records . The State of Michigan’s own index to its births, marriages and deaths. Michigan County Histories and Atlases . The University of Michigan’s free scans of the county histories, Rogers, Mathews and Glover among them. Find a Grave . Free transcriptions and photographs of gravestones. Read the stone on paper. Tip: read every box, including the small print at the bottom. Ages are often given to the day, in years, months and days. Count back from the date of death and you have a birth date to check against everything else. Just remember the informant gave that age too. t: Paw Paw, Michigan history and records
x: ← The places Van Buren County, Michigan Paw Paw, Michigan: its history, in the record Paw Paw, the seat of Van Buren County, takes its name from the Paw Paw River and the pawpaw trees that grew along it. Rodney Hinckley took up a farm on the river in 1832, a sawmill followed in 1833, and the village was incorporated in 1837; the Van Buren County Courthouse on Paw Paw Street is on the National Register of Historic Places. The town at a glance Founded: settled 1832–33; incorporated 1837; the county seat. Name: from the Paw Paw River, itself named for the pawpaw tree. In the record: Ellis’s history of Berrien and Van Buren counties (1880) and Rowland’s of Van Buren (1912); the Paw Paw True Northerner, from the 1850s. On the map: the 1860 Geil & Harley county map carries a plan of Paw Paw; lay it over today’s streets . Wine country: grapes are the district’s crop; St. Julian and Warner Vineyards both began in Paw Paw, and the village holds a Wine and Harvest Festival each autumn. On old postcards Old Van Buren County Courthouse, Paw Paw (engraving) · 1880, D.W. Ensign & Co. none required · source From public-domain postcards and photographs, each linked to the library that holds it. See them all . Where to look The county seat’s records — probate, deeds and the True Northerner — are the first stop for Van Buren families; the 1912 Rowland history is the fullest for the townships. t: How the valley’s towns got their names
x: ← Project Scroll · All the news A series How the valley’s towns got their names Every town in the valley has a story about its name, and most of the stories are only half the record. In this series we go back to the plats, the acts, the post-office lists and the county histories for each one: the oldest spellings, the legends against the record, and what nobody wrote down. Press a town on the map to read its story. 7 towns so far. State outline: U.S. Census Bureau, via us-atlas; rivers: Natural Earth (public domain), simplified. Kalamazoo A footrace, a cherry tree, a missing letter L, and the oldest spelling on paper. Cassopolis A governor’s name, a Greek word, a race through the rain, and the A that became an O. Dowagiac A creek’s name, a railroad town, a paper town called Venice, and two meanings. Niles Pog-wa-tigue, a Baltimore editor, a plat recorded in Lenawee County, and three flags, one of them for a day or less. Edwardsburg Beardsley’s Prairie, a storekeeper, a major, and a disputed Edwards. Paw Paw A river, a tree, an English word, and a township called Lafayette. Vandalia A post office, a Quaker mill, a missionary’s wife, and a name nobody explained. Which town should be next? Tell us , and send any record of a name’s origin you know of. t: Old postcards and photographs of the valley
x: ← The map room Postcards, then and now Stand where the photographer stood Old postcards of Cassopolis, from the days of wagons to the first motor cars. Each one was taken from a spot you can still stand on. Find it, take the same picture today, and send it to us: we will set your photograph beside the old one here, with your name on it. West side of Broadway, looking south. A Yerty postcard. The photographer stood on Broadway with the stores of the west side on the right. Find it on the 1860 plan → Broadway in the days of wagons. Horses and wagons on the main street, the store fronts close together. Find it on the 1860 plan → Carriages drawn up on Broadway. A row of buggies at the hitching rail: a market day, or a meeting. Find it on the 1860 plan → Broadway when the first cars came. Early motor cars among the last of the buggies. Find it on the 1860 plan → A Cassopolis street, early 1900s. Which street is it? The trees, the walks and the buildings are the clues. Find it on the 1860 plan → The road to town. The way in from the country. Where did it come in, and is the road still there? Find it on the 1860 plan → How to rephotograph a postcard Find the spot. Line up two things that have not moved, a corner of a building and a street, and walk until they sit in the picture the way they sit on the card. Match the height. Most old postcards were taken from about head height; some from an upstairs window. Hold the camera where the photographer’s eye was. Match the lens. Use your phone’s ordinary camera, not the wide one, and do not zoom. Stay safe and on public ground. Never step into the road for a shot, and never go onto private property without leave. Send it in to research@projectscroll.com , saying which card and when you took it. By sending it you let us show it here with your name. The pictures are taken from old postcards of Cassopolis. Each was published before 1931, or published without a copyright notice, and is in the public domain in the United States. The pairings will be added as readers send them in. Then and now: your photographs The first pair is waiting for you. Take the same picture as one of these postcards, from the same spot, and send it in. Your photograph will go here beside the old one, with a slider to move between then and now, and your name under it. The valley on old postcards and photographs 121 more views of the towns of the St. Joseph River valley, from Cassopolis to Michigan City: main streets, depots, courthouses, libraries, hotels, mills, fairs and parades, most of them between 1900 and 1930. Each one links to the library or archive that holds it. Press a picture to see it full size. ← Project Scroll Privacy What this site keeps Almost nothing. Project Scroll has no accounts and no ads of its own. One thing is optional and off until you say yes: a visit counter from Meta, used to see how the hunt is found and, later, to show Project Scroll’s own advertisements to people who have been here. You choose on your first visit, and you can change your mind here. Your choice on this device: not made yet Kept in your own browser A few things are remembered so the site works the way you left it. They are stored in your browser on this device, nobody else can see them, and we never receive them. Light or dark. The page colors you chose. The lantern. Whether you put it out. The opening flourish. That you have already seen the ink draw itself on your first visit, so it does not replay. Your tin badges. The badges you have earned around the site, and the days you visited, so the “Regular” badge can count them. Your followed cases. The cases you starred on the case board. Your case notes. Anything you write in a case notebook. See all your notes . Your answer about the visit counter. Allow or keep off, so you are not asked again. Your drafts. What you type into the message form and the family-history and family-legend forms, so it survives a reload. Nothing is sent from those forms; you copy the text and send it yourself. To clear all of it, clear this site’s data in your browser settings. Sent to other sites Where am I? On a then-and-now page, the “Where am I?” button asks your device for its location so it can put a dot on the old plan. The location is used only in your browser, to draw the dot. It is never sent to Project Scroll or stored. Today’s names. On a then-and-now page, once you have solved its renamed-street challenge, the “Today’s names” switch shows OpenStreetMap’s own map under the old plan. Only when you turn it on does your browser ask OpenStreetMap’s tile server (tile.openstreetmap.org) for those map pieces, under its privacy policy . The map room. The 1860 wall map is shown straight from the Library of Congress, so your browser asks the Library’s image server (tile.loc.gov) for the pieces of the map you look at. The other county maps in the map room come the same way from the University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee Libraries (cdm17272.contentdm.oclc.org) and the University of Michigan Library (quod.lib.umich.edu). The Sanborn sheets and the Cassopolis page’s 1884 corner come from Wikimedia Commons (commons.wikimedia.org and its image servers). The 1860 half of the Penn Township slider on the Cassopolis page comes from the same server. Facebook. Links to Project Scroll’s Facebook pages and Messenger simply take you there. On a case page you can choose to show the live Facebook post; only then does your browser load it from Facebook, under Facebook’s own terms. Until you click, nothing from Facebook is loaded. The Meta visit counter (only if you allow it). If you choose “Allow”, your browser loads a small script from Meta (the Meta Pixel) that tells Meta which pages of this site you looked at, and when. Meta may match that to a Facebook or Instagram account if you have one, under Meta’s privacy policy . We use it to see which parts of the hunt and the studio are visited, and later to show Project Scroll’s own advertisements on Facebook and Instagram to people who have been here. It records page views, when the Services section is read, and when the Messenger button is pressed. It never sees what you type: your notes, drafts and messages stay in your browser as before. If you choose “Keep it off”, or make no choice, nothing from Meta is loaded, and nothing is counted. When you write to us Email to research@projectscroll.com lands in a mailbox hosted for us by GoDaddy on Microsoft 365, under GoDaddy’s privacy policy ; messages sent through Facebook travel under Facebook’s own terms. Either way, what you tell us about your family is used to answer your question and for nothing else, and is never sold or shared. B

Based in the St. Joseph River Valley of southwest Michigan and northern Indiana, working anywhere the records reach. What we research Lost ancestors. One clear question, answered from certificates, deeds, censuses, county histories, maps and newspapers, every statement marked with its source. Family histories and registers. Every descendant of one couple, or every ancestor of one person, built from the records and written to be checked. See a specimen . Family legends tested. The famous ancestor, the three brothers who came over together, the land that was taken. We find where the story began and what the records say. How it works . Where we work Cass, Berrien, Van Buren and St. Joseph counties in Michigan; St. Joseph and Elkhart counties in Indiana; and, wherever the records are online, anywhere. We read the Michigan county histories, the General Land Office tract books and plats, Michigan and Indiana vital records, and the newspapers of the St. Joseph River Valley as a matter of course. ← The map room Roads, rails, bridges and mills How the valley was joined First came the canals that were never dug and the plank roads that were. Then the bridges over the St. Joseph, and at last the iron road, which decided which towns would grow and which would wait. Here it is in the order it happened, each date from the county histories with its page. The dates 26 March 1835 Niles. A charter was granted to Obed P. Lacey for a toll bridge over the St. Joseph at Niles. History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties, Michigan (D. W. Ensign, 1880), p. 159 8 December 1835 Niles. Citizens met at Edwardsburg about a canal from Constantine to Niles; most of those present favored a railroad. Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), p. 79 21 March 1836 Niles. Niles obtained a charter for a free bridge across the St. Joseph River. History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties, Michigan (D. W. Ensign, 1880), p. 159 26 March 1836 Constantine. ← Project Scroll Soldiers of the valley Company D, Sixth Michigan Infantry In the summer of 1861 a company was raised at Dowagiac, the second organized in Cass County. Here are its 85 men as the county history printed them in 1882: who they were, how they served, and how 19 of them did not come home. The company’s war Raised at Dowagiac, summer 1861, under Capt. Charles E. Clarke, with Frederick J. Clarke as first lieutenant. The regiment gathered at Kalamazoo and left for the East on 30 August 1861, 944 strong. Mathews, p. 117 Baltimore, then the Mississippi. After garrison duty at Baltimore it went to New Orleans and the lower Mississippi, fought at Baton Rouge on 5 August 1862, and in the assault on Port Hudson on 27 May 1863, where Lieutenant Frederick Clarke was killed. pp. 117–118 Heavy artillery. After Port Hudson the regiment became heavy artillery, served at Fort Morgan and in the siege of Mobile, and was paid off and discharged at Jackson, Michigan, on 5 September 1865. p. 118 Of the men below, 4 were killed or died of wounds and 15 died of disease: at Baltimore, New Orleans, Baton Rouge, Carrollton and, most of all, in the hot summer at Port Hudson. Disease killed more soldiers than battle in this war, and this company is no exception. New: The libraries behind the stories : every library, archive and newspaper our news stories draw on, and which stories use each one. County histories How far to trust them. Written a generation or two after the events, mostly from the recollections of old settlers, and paid for by subscribers whose biographies they print. Rich in names and dates, wrong often enough that every fact should be checked against a deed, a census or a newspaper. Howard S. Rogers, History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 (Cassopolis: W. H. Mansfield, 1875). University of Michigan Library The earliest county history, closest to the first settlers. Short, and often the source the later books copy. Alfred Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (Chicago: Waterman, Watkins & Co., 1882). University of Michigan Library Much longer, with township and village histories and biographies. Repeats Rogers in places, adds new witnesses in others; its footnotes say who told what. L. H. Glover, A Twentieth Century History of Cass County, Michigan (Chicago: Lewis Publishing, 1906). University of Michigan Library The county as it stood a generation later. Good on churches, schools and businesses of its day; leans on the earlier books for the pioneer years. Portrait and Biographical Record of Berrien and Cass Counties, Michigan (Chicago: Biographical Publishing Co., 1893). Subscription biographies, written with the families. Strong on births, marriages and children; kind to its subjects. County and town maps How far to trust them. Landownership maps were sold by subscription, so the names on the farms and the directories beside the town plans are the people who paid. The streets, lots and buildings are usually true to the ground; the names are a snapshot of one year. ← Project Scroll The hunter’s toolkit Tools for reading the record Four small tools we use at the desk every day, and a cipher wheel for the hunt. They run entirely in your browser: nothing you type or load here is sent anywhere. Faded-ink enhancer Load a photo of an old letter, deed, certificate or page. Slide until the writing stands out, then save the clearer copy. Your photo never leaves your device. Choose a photo No photo chosen. Brightness Contrast Lift faded ink Sharpen Black and white Invert (light writing on dark) Age at death → birth date Old certificates and gravestones often give age to the day: “aged 71 years, 4 months, 12 days.” Count back from the date of death and you have a birth date to test against everything else. Date of death Years Months Days Remember: the informant gave that age, so it is a clue to test, not a proof. Stones carved years later can be off too. Soundex finder The indexes to the 1880 to 1930 censuses, made in the 1930s and 1940s, were filed by Soundex, a code that groups surnames that sound alike. Type a surname to get its code and spellings worth searching. Surname Cousin calculator Start from the ancestor two people share. Say how each one descends from that ancestor, and the calculator names the relationship. The town's history museum began at Southwestern Michigan College and moved downtown in 2013, taking over a building that had held retail shops. Its biggest story is the Round Oak Stove Company, which Philo D. Beckwith incorporated in 1871 after casting his first stove around 1867 to heat his own foundry; the company stopped making stoves in 1946 and its buildings were sold in 1947. Now. A free museum (Tuesday-Friday 10-5, Saturday 10-2) with about 4,000 square feet of exhibits, including what is described as the largest public collection of Round Oak heating stoves in the world. 201 E. Division St., Dowagiac, MI 49047 source 1 source 2 source 3 source 4 source 5 source 6 · Open the Sanborn sheets of Dowagiac Stop 2 of 13 The Heddon Museum Then. The museum tells the story of James Heddon, who in the late 1890s whittled a piece of wood while waiting by the Mill Pond, saw a bass strike it when he tossed it in, and went on to make a top-water lure he named the Dowagiac. James Heddon's Sons ran from 1902 to 1984 and by the 1920s was the world's biggest maker of quality fishing tackle, also turning out golf shafts, ski poles, violin bows, box kites and, in World War II, radio antennae. Now. A volunteer-run museum of the Dowagiac Area History Museum (open Tuesday and Friday, 10-5; call ahead) with more than 1,000 lures, 140 reels and 150 rods. 115 S. Front St., Dowagiac, MI 49047 source 1 source 2 source 3 · Open the Sanborn sheets of Dowagiac Stop 3 of 13 · by 1899 The Fair Store block Then. A store called The Fair was here by 1899, when the city directory listed Emanuel Tobias as its owner. The block then held a run of other businesses until 1941, when The Fair came back as a large department store that kept its doors open into the 1970s. Now. Present occupant not confirmed. 117-123 S. Front St., Dowagiac, MI 49047 source 1 source 2 · Open the Sanborn sheets of Dowagiac Stop 4 of 13 · built 1892 (theatre opened 19 January 1893; razed 1966) Beckwith Park and the Beckwith Memorial Theatre site The Beckwith Building, Dowagiac, on a postcard of about 1912 Tinder Collection, Clements Library, University of Michigan · source 📷 Photo spot. Open park ground from 1848, this corner became the site of the Beckwith Memorial in 1892, built in memory of Round Oak founder P. D. Beckwith by his daughter and son-in-law, in Lake Superior red sandstone, and dedicated in January 1893. Besides a 600-seat theatre counted among the finest between New York and Chicago, the building held a bank, city hall and the Round Oak company offices; films were shown from 1914. It was torn down in 1966, and a bank building later stood on part of the lot; the city bought that in 2019, took it down in 2020 and added the ground to the park. Now. Beckwith Park, renovated and reopened in July 2021. A piece of the theatre's red sandstone wall still shows on the building next door. Southeast corner of S. Cass County’s first courthouse was a plain wooden building, 34 by 24 feet, ordered by the county board in 1835 for about $450 and built by Joseph Harper. All three county histories put it on Lot 4, Block 2 north, Range 1 west of the village plat: the west side of Broadway, in the second block north of State Street. It served until the second courthouse opened in 1841. Now. Nothing of it survives. This stop marks that stretch of Broadway; the exact building line is not known. West side of North Broadway, second block north of State Street source 1 source 2 source 3 source 4 source 5 source 6 · The square on the 1884 Sanborn sheet Stop 2 of 11 · built 1908-1909 Local History Branch (Carnegie Library) The Public Library, Cassopolis, on a postcard of 1914 Tinder Collection, Clements Library, University of Michigan · source 📷 Photo spot. Stand where the photographer stood: line up the rooflines and corners with the postcard, take the same picture, and send it to us . The best go up beside the old view, with your name. Then. Built over the winter of 1908-09 with a $10,000 gift from Andrew Carnegie, this was the town’s public library for more than 80 years; Cassopolis was one of 53 Michigan communities to receive Carnegie library money. From 1947 to 1957 its basement also housed the Cass County Library, and after the 1993 merger that created the Cass District Library it reopened in October 1994 as the Local History Branch. Now. The Cass District Library's Local History Branch, a genealogy and county-history research library (Mon-Thu 9-4), restored in 2012 and renovated again in 2020-21. 145 N. The stone courthouse with its tall clock tower was designed by the Grand Rapids firm Rush, Bowman & Rush and finished in 1900 by the contractors James Rowson and August Mohnke, after the county dismissed its first builder in 1898. It cost $43,797.88 with furniture and heating, and stands on the northeast quarter of the old public square, where the 1841 courthouse stood for nearly sixty years. The county jail of 1852 stood just north of it. Now. Empty after the courts moved out in 2003, it was restored with federal ARPA and USDA money and reopened in October 2024 as county offices: administrator, clerk/register of deeds, treasurer and the Board of Commissioners. 120 N. Built in 1860, this brick building held the county’s offices — the clerk, the probate court, the register of deeds and the treasurer — until the stone courthouse across the way was finished in 1899. The supervisors ordered it built fireproof, after a fire in the village had alarmed them about the county’s records.
